items.title: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away
items.author: Kyle Orland
items.summary: How do you think you're going to die? If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident." In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. Read full article Comments

items.title: Longer inhibitory connections can push simulated neural networks beyond critical tipping point
items.summary: In neuroscience, the brain criticality hypothesis proposes that neurons in the brain are arranged in such a way that neural activity lies at or near a transition point between two extremes: an ordered state where neural activity dies out quickly and a disordered state where neural activity tends to spread quickly and potentially grow uncontrollably. This transition point is known as criticality, while the two activity regimes on either side of it are known as subcritical and supercritical, respectively.

items.title: Pharmaceutical ads may influence which drug AI recommends, new research finds
items.author: Sarah Hofmann
items.summary: Next time you ask AI for medical advice, you may want to consider whether it’s been influenced by Big Pharma. Prescription drug advertisements are everywhere, and may affect AI’s recommendations, according to a study published in The Lancet Digital Health this week. The study authors conducted experiments with a dozen consumer-facing LLMs, including versions of Claude, Gemini, and GPT—made by Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, respectively. Clinical guidance or commercial influence? The models were tested across 33 scenarios that each included a clinical case description and multiple treatment options. In some cases, the AI models were also given an ad for one of the treatment options. The ad’s content included information about the drug and its uses, but did not specifically direct the AI model to recommend the drug. When AI models were exposed to an ad, they recommended the treatment in question an average 47.6% of the time, compared to 35% when no ad was present, though the shifts varied between the 12 models. Although the models often changed their recommendation when an ad was present, in most cases, they still selected one of the appropriate options. The outputs only disclosed th

Researchers at Stanford University found that adults with type 2 diabetes who were taking metformin before catching COVID-19 had a 39% lower risk of dying in the year following their infection than patients taking a different type of diabetes medication . The findings, published in the journal Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, point to potential protective effects that go beyond basic glucose control. Metformin lowers blood sugar and helps the body use insulin more effectively, though it's unclear whether these effects explain the study’s findings. Researchers noted that the drug may help regulate a biological pathway involved in blood pressure and fluid balance that influences the severity of COVID-19. items.title: Android TV box malware found in 1.3M devices
items.summary: You buy a streaming box, plug it into your television and connect it to Wi-Fi. A few minutes later, you're watching your favorite show. Everything seems perfectly normal. But what if that little box has been secretly working for criminals since the day you brought it home? That's the alarming discovery behind a massive Android TV box malware operation involving more than 1.3 million devices worldwide. According to a Nov. 2 report from Google's Threat Intelligence Group, investigators concluded with high confidence that a device manufacturer deliberately installed hidden software inside streaming hardware. That backdoor gave outsiders remote access without the owners knowing. And here's what makes this particularly concerning. The malware was built directly into the devices, and some affected products made it through Google's own security certification process. items.summary: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. When it comes to reading, I’m not a glutton for punishment—I didn’t get very far into Finnegans Wake —but I am drawn to interesting challenges. Among the most memorably difficult reads I’ve taken on was the 1926 book A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle . A cerebral but darkly funny epic poem whose plot is well summarized by its title, it is written in “synthetic Scots,” a language cobbled together from Scottish dialects by its author, Hugh MacDiarmid. (Although Scots survives as a minority language with many regional variations, none of them closely resemble MacDiarmid’s concoction.) I loved the verse for its woozy lyricism and nerded out on the text’s annotations; I was also fascinated by the author’s grand ambitions. MacDiarmid was part of a cultural movement known as the Scottish Renaissance, whose writers sought to revive the once-independent nation’s dialects and traditions. But did he really think he could kick off a national resurgence by inventing a language no reader could easily understand? And what would drive a writer to even try? items.title: The Guardian view on M John Harrison’s Booker win: a new frontier for science fiction | Editorial
items.author: Editorial
items.summary: The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past “Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize. Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t want to break out of the ghetto; he wants to break it down. “I really hate categories, and I really hate being categorised,” he said .

Yet until last month, even she was unaware of a major and concerning piece of news: her own conviction. In 2024, a court issued her a one-year sentence for “spreading false news” and running a website without a licence – which she had repeatedly sought to obtain – after trying her in absentia, even though she was in the country. Ms Attalah learned of the case only after she was separately tried in October , resulting in a large fine and an order for the closure of the Mada Masr website. She faces retrial later this month. Meanwhile, the entire newsroom of the fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention weeks after authorities snatched the six journalists on charges including joining and financing a terrorist group and spreading false news. Their lawyers say that they have been tortured and forced to record fabricated confessions.

The big picture: Many crucial global goods are built on supply chains that have one or more Achilles' heels, a report from the consulting firm McKinsey finds — a critical input, concentrated suppliers and geopolitical strain. That manifests partly in physical chokepoints. The Strait of Hormuz is the one most in the news, but the McKinsey researchers identify a couple dozen others globally, through which 80% of maritime trade passes (although with varying levels of difficulty for shippers to route around). In effect, as the global economy has become more integrated over the last few decades, these vulnerabilities have become more pronounced — which in turn helps explain why the 2020s have brought an ongoing series of disruptive supply shocks. items.title: Gen Z hasn’t made up its mind on AI, survey finds
items.author: J.D. Capelouto
items.summary: Gen Z is often cast as souring on AI, but they’re no more negative about the technology than their parents and grandparents. A new survey from Milltown Partners, shared first with Semafor, found that 73% of Gen Z adults haven’t made up their minds on AI, while half said they expect AI to harm society. That matches baby boomers (50%) and Gen Xers (48%), while millennials were the most upbeat, with 39% expecting harm. Companies and politicians are all eager to understand the generation’s stance on AI, given how much they drive tech trends and how AI and data centers played an outsize role in the US midterm election. The report also pointed to a paradox that seems to define young people’s relationship with AI: Many say it makes them worse at thinking for themselves and harder to find a job — but 46% said they use it every day, the second-highest rate behind millennials. Young people are also less worried than older generations about the existential risk that dominates much of the AI safety discourse. And they are more conflicted about their own use: 30% of Gen Zers said they sometimes feel guilty using AI, more than double the rate among respondents over 30.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s biggest mistake was getting too involved in DC

items.summary: Reed’s view Jensen Huang made a lot of mistakes, but the one that really brought him down was getting too involved in DC. The skillset of a great technologist is the opposite of someone who’s great at politics. Technologists have to think years, sometimes decades in advance. When they figure out a winning formula, they bet everything on it. That’s a really bad way to operate in Washington, where things move on two-year election cycles and commitment to any one idea, faction, or ideology is a liability if and when the political winds change. When Donald Trump was elected president for a second term, it seemed like the world was suddenly a fundamentally different place. The White House was open for business in a way never seen in history. It was irresistible for a lot of tech people (Elon Musk and Marc Andreessen also fell into this trap). For a while, it seemed like Huang was one of the few technologists to find success in DC. His friendship with the president helped advance his worldview — that America should export its technology around the world, even to China. But it was all a mirage. items.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.summary: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates. Millions of people around the world take these medications – including 30 million in the U.S. – to treat diabetes and obesity and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. items.title: A digital bank’s collapse toppled Paraguay’s president within days — and cracked the myth of the ‘Dubai of South America’
items.author: Joel E. Correia, The Conversation
items.summary: It started on Nov. 3, 2026, when millions of Paraguayans trying to access the Ueno banking app found they could no longer get their money . In a matter of days, the financial situation escalated into political crisis, in which the country’s president was ousted, placed under house arrest and charged with several corruption-related crimes. The political and financial crisis exposes a central contradiction in Paraguay’s recent economic development . Ueno, a bank celebrated for expanding financial access to ordinary Paraguayans, grew through unusually close relationships with political elites and public institutions. Gerrymandering has obvious implications for fairness and democracy, characterized by some as politicians picking their voters, not voters picking their politicians. There’s also a practical consideration for those doing the gerrymandering: The efforts can fail when they overplay their hand. By spreading their supportive voters across many districts, parties can create more seats that may lean in their direction. items.title: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
items.author: Jennifer Ouellette
items.summary: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point. It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. items.title: Climate Advisers director: The U.S. needs a clean energy standard for AI data centers
items.author: Matt Piotrowski
items.summary: Voters delivered a verdict on data centers in the midterm election. In an NBC News exit poll, 56% said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, and voters passed more than 40 local measures restricting data centers. Lawmakers now face a choice. They can answer with bans, or with rules that decide who pays for AI’s power but ignore where it comes from. Either would be half a policy. Voters want lower bills and cleaner air, and clean energy can address both. Ireland, Singapore and China have already tied data center growth to clean power. The United States should too. Residents outside Memphis have seen the alternative. xAI has run dozens of gas turbines across the state line in Southaven, Mississippi, to power its Colossus 2 data center, drawing lawsuits and complaints over air quality . More are coming. Global Energy Monitor counts 189 GW of natural gas tied to data centers in development as of mid-2026, with about 17 GW already under construction . items.title: Democrats won Congress. Now they must win back trade policy
items.author: Desirée LeClercq
items.summary: Days after winning Congress, Democrats are debating whether and how to restore congressional authority over tariffs. Some in the party are focusing on reining in Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs on allies like Canada, while others hope that a 2029 Democratic President might direct Trump’s expansive tariffs toward progressive priorities, such as raising labor standards. This debate is missing two things. First, it blames trade failures on Trump, when both the Trump and Biden administrations pursued similar trade policies that failed workers. Second, it focuses on taking tariff power back from the president but overlooks Congress’s role in setting trade objectives. I have spent my career trying to make trade work for American workers. As a progressive, I urge congressional Democrats to take stock of the lessons from both the Trump and Biden administrations, which requires a course correction, even if it means restraining a future Democratic president. Both administrations, acting unilaterally, have cost us. Congress once shared control over trade policy. Among the things Slate does without is an embedded infotainment system. The small digital display on the dashboard that shows your speed and range is also where the backup camera appears if you engage reverse, and there are two USB-C ports that provide power but not connectivity, and that’s that. items.title: Scientists warn 1.5°C climate change threshold could arrive by 2029
items.author: Bob Berwyn, Inside Climate News
items.summary: ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming. Climate Action Tracker , a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement . When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus. Read full article Comments

items.title: Opinion: New organ donation rules are unfair to families
items.author: Tarvez Tucker
items.summary: I watched Hailey’s chest without pause, searching for the slightest movement, a tiny intake of breath, any sign of life. Hailey (not her real name) was 22 years old, a college student who had suffered a catastrophic brain injury in a traffic accident. She lay before me in our neuroscience intensive care unit, her heart beating steadily, her skin warm, a ventilator breathing for her. I was performing an apnea test, the final step in determining whether she had died by neurological criteria. It’s part of my job as a neurointensivist at Oregon Health & Science University. The longest 10 minutes of my life are those I spend watching for any small chest movement as we remove a patient from a breathing machine. I can’t let my eyes wander. I can’t blink. It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business. items.title: DR Congo president enacts referendum law
items.author: Ruben Nyanguila
items.summary: DR Congo’s president has signed a law allowing the constitution to be changed or replaced through a referendum, a move opponents warn could pave the way for him to seek a third term in the mineral-rich country. Félix Tshisekedi, in power since 2019, is due to complete his second and final term under the current constitution in just over two years. He said in May he was not seeking constitutional changes to stay in power, but would accept a third term if the Congolese people wanted it. The country was ruled by dictator Mobutu Sese Seko for three decades until his overthrow in 1997. After years of war, its 2006 constitution introduced safeguards against a return to dictatorship, including presidential term limits. But Tshisekedi’s predecessor, Joseph Kabila, still stayed in office for two years after his final term expired. Opposition leaders have joined forces to resist any attempt to extend Tshisekedi’s rule, organizing protests at home and seeking support from European governments. They argue that a referendum cannot override the constitution’s ban on changing presidential term limits. — Ruben Nyanguila

Presenting the budget, the finance minister told lawmakers “too little value” was added domestically. As part of the push to shift the economy, Africa’s largest gold producer wants to phase out exports of unprocessed minerals by 2030. Much of the skilled employment linked to its mineral wealth currently takes place abroad, the finance ministry says. The government is targeting economic growth of 8% by 2030 and the budget has allocated $2.6 billion to support agriculture, energy, and manufacturing over the next year. Ghana completed an IMF bailout program this year and now plans to repay about $3 billion in domestic and international debt ahead of schedule. — Ruben Nyanguila

items.title: Nvidia’s next CEO will have to keep an entire industry alive

items.summary: Reed’s view Nvidia got caught without a succession plan for CEO Jensen Huang, but it wasn’t for lack of trying, according to people briefed on the effort to hire a replacement. Before the 63-year-old founder was ousted, the company did try to hire an external number two, according to a person familiar with the search. It was difficult to find candidates, though, because none wanted to work in Huang’s shadow. The Huang hangover might still be a problem even after he’s gone. There’s a Slack group at the company, for instance, titled “Stand with Jensen,” and people familiar with the search process estimate there are fewer than 10 people in the world truly capable of running the company. The next Nvidia CEO doesn’t just have to keep its own products shipping on time. The person who takes the top job also has to keep the entire industry alive. There’s really no replacing him . Notable Several names have been floated for who could replace Huang, including Apple’s hardware chief Johny Srouji, Arm CEO Rene Haas, or even, on President Donald Trump’s suggestion , former Apple CEO Tim Cook.

items.summary: Artificial intelligence is going to disrupt insurance brokerage. There is not much question about that. The question that matters is what gets disrupted, and how differently firms are preparing for it. Most firms are approaching AI the way they approached every prior wave of technology: take the work as it exists and do it faster. But AI is dramatically changing the economics of gathering information, comparing coverage and facilitating transactions. A firm whose value lives in those activities is competing in a race to the bottom. A firm built on specialized expertise, deep client relationships and experiential human judgment can change the paradigm, turning risk into opportunity for clients. Firms that make that leap go from being a vendor of downside protection to a business partner that helps a client achieve the fullness of their ambition. Their value becomes constrained only by what their clients can achieve. Showing up that way requires the fortitude to completely rebuild how the work gets done. items.author: Johnny Kauffman
items.summary: On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. But it’s time to start looking at the Rust Belt city as a warning about the future. As the artificial intelligence revolution unfolds, debates about its impact on the American economy often hinge on the belief that if the technology creates more jobs than it destroys, it will be a success. But the more important question is often the most overlooked: Who will bear the costs of the AI revolution? Youngstown is a symbol for what can happen when America stands idly by as market forces inflict abrupt economic transition on communities. And the next Youngstown may already be taking shape. It may not depend on a steel mill, but on concentrations of jobs increasingly vulnerable to AI. From Huntsville, Texas, to State College, Pennsylvania, the industries will be different, but the risk is familiar: jobs transformed or eliminated faster than the community around them can adapt. items.title: Why BMI Is Not the Best Measure of Health
items.author: Alice Park
items.summary: —Jupiterimages—Getty Images BMI, or body mass index, has long been a part of health evaluations. A calculation that takes into account a person’s weight and height, BMI is supposed to reflect how much excess fat a person might be carrying and give doctors a sense of a patient's risk for obesity-related health conditions. For years, however, doctors have found that BMI isn’t the best measure of obesity-related health, since it can’t distinguish between fat and muscle weight. items.title: Ancient tunnels beneath famous Hagia Sophia explored after 3,000 tons of debris cleared
items.summary: Archaeologists have removed roughly 3,000 tons of debris from a centuries-old network of underground tunnels beneath Istanbul's iconic Hagia Sophia — revealing previously inaccessible passages beneath one of the world's most historic religious landmarks. The findings were announced by archaeologist Hasan Fırat Diker at a presentation this fall in Istanbul, as local outlet Türkiye Today reported. The tunnels have been undergoing excavation and clearing work since February 2025, allowing researchers to explore sections that were previously buried beneath mud and debris. NOAH'S ARK SITE YIELDS FIRST LOOK AT CHARRED WOOD FRAGMENTS RECOVERED DEEP BELOW SOIL During the Oct. 16 presentation, Diker said the roughly 1,600-year-old tunnels were built by the Romans and originally functioned as part of the city's water distribution and drainage network, while also providing a protected underground space. Some of the underground structures predate the present-day Hagia Sophia, which was completed in 537 A.D. under Byzantine Emperor Justinian I. Elizabeth Holmes hadn’t even considered politics before 2026, and within months, she unseated Meg Weinberger, a Donald Trump–endorsed Republican known as “MAGA Meg” who had won the seat in 2024. Earlier this year, Weinberger sponsored legislation to rename the Palm Beach airport after the president, a project that cost $5.5 million . Holmes’ win there highlights how the MAGA movement is losing some of its power—even in the county Trump calls home. The genesis of Holmes’ dizzyingly rapid campaign and victory can be traced back to April 15, an especially hard day at work. One of Holmes’ special education students ended up in the hospital after a mental health crisis. When Holmes got home later that day, she saw the news that during union contract negotiations, the superintendent offered the district’s teachers a 1.5 percent raise—a far cry from the 3.5 percent they’d been hoping for. Recordings of private calls and events reviewed by ProPublica show current and former state board members working with the Election Integrity Network and allied organizations on shared priorities. items.summary: The Scene When Massachusetts-based Commonwealth Fusion Systems looked for companies that could produce large metal components and complex machinery for its prototype, it landed on the oil and gas industry. CEO Bob Mumgaard said the hydrocarbons industry shares many of the same skills and tools that fusion developers need to achieve a breakthrough and eventually take a share of the energy mix. The UAE is well positioned to use its expertise in oil and gas to adopt fusion technology, Mumgaard said, especially after it has developed a track record of building nuclear power plants and its embrace of AI. “They understand what energy leadership and first mover advantage, advanced technologies can bring to their society, their place in the world,” he said. Abu Dhabi’s government-owned fusion fund, Plynth Energy, acquired a minority stake worth more than $100 million in Commonwealth this year, according to Axios. The US company raised $1 billion in July, bringing its total funding to $4 billion, which Mumgaard said would be enough to build the prototype and prepare for a larger, utility-scale plant in the early 2030s. items.title: EU AI summit expected to be overshadowed by Ukraine war
items.author: Prashant Rao
items.summary: European leaders were set to hold talks on how to compete with the US and China in the AI race, but analysts voiced skepticism the EU could overcome structural shortcomings. The summit in Dublin, the first of its kind to focus solely on AI, is expected to be overshadowed by debate over financial support for Ukraine, discussion over who speaks for the bloc internationally, and horse-trading over an EU-wide budget. The EU’s efforts on AI have in any case so far been scattershot and largely fallen shy of their stated targets . Europe is “a large economy but clearly far behind the US and China,” one leading analyst noted recently, “ which is why it has no seat at the table .” — Prashant Rao

items.title: FTC to block $3.5B veterinary merger
items.author: Rohan Goswami
items.summary: The Scoop The FTC is flexing its regulatory muscle again. The antitrust regulator is planning to file suit to block a $3.5 billion veterinary deal later today, according to people familiar with the matter, seeking to prevent a private equity-owned company from acquiring a smaller rival. The regulator plans to cite increased costs for pet owners and veterinary clinics as part of the suit to block CD&R and TPG-owned Covetrus from acquiring MWI Veterinary Supply, the people said. Covetrus and MWI are both national suppliers of medical supplies and products. The Commission believes that the combination would result in a highly concentrated market, the people said. Neither Covetrus nor MWI returned a request for comment. Rohan’s view Under Andrew Ferguson, the FTC, unlike the Justice Department, has managed to focus on its regulatory mission — even if it has allowed many mergers to pass uncontested. It has used its enforcement tools to execute President Donald Trump’s agenda, which has recently centered on affordability. It is that focus, Washington insiders say, that has now given Ferguson a degree of latitude to pursue cases and merger enforcement that he desires. The FTC is also plan

items.title: Gaming industry poll finds most Americans see prediction markets as gambling
items.author: Eleanor Mueller
items.summary: A bipartisan 82% majority of Americans think that prediction markets should be regulated as gambling products instead of financial ones, a poll conducted by Qualtrics on behalf of the American Gaming Association found. The poll also found that 75% say using the markets to buy and sell sports-related event contracts is the same as using a sportsbook to bet on sports. The group is using the findings, shared first with Semafor , to reinforce its argument that states and tribes should oversee the markets instead of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission ahead of a looming Supreme Court ruling . “In an era of political division, Americans are overwhelmingly united against Kalshi’s deceptive marketing of sports gambling as investing,” AGA President and CEO Bill Miller said.

items.title: Demand remains strong for Anthropic IPO despite tech pullback
items.author: Jeronimo Gonzalez
items.summary: Anthropic’s IPO is reportedly six times oversubscribed , reflecting bullishness on the AI trade despite recent headwinds. Fears of overspending and soaring debt piles have led investors to pull out from tech stocks in recent weeks, with the Nasdaq index registering its biggest monthly loss in over a year in October. The resignation of the CEO of Nvidia, a firm that has underpinned much of the global AI buildout, has amplified concerns. However, some investors appear undaunted, likely owing to upbeat predictions for future growth: Goldman Sachs, one of the banks leading Anthropic’s IPO, said it expected the firm’s revenue to exceed $600 billion by 2030, more than 130 times its sales last year. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

items.title: Nigeria election body to comply with presidential candidate ruling
items.author: Alexis Akwagyiram
items.summary: The News Nigeria’s electoral commission will obey any court ruling on whether the main challenger to President Bola Tinubu is eligible to contest January’s presidential election, its chairman said, potentially handing the judiciary a key role in Africa’s biggest poll. Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar is set to appeal last week’s high court ruling that invalidated his candidacy . The chair of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Joash Amupitan, speaking at the Chatham House think tank in London, said the body would be constitutionally “obligated” to “obey every court order” if the appeal fails. INEC’s position adds to uncertainty around the vote in Africa’s top crude oil producer with less than 10 weeks until polls open.The commission is currently embroiled in more than 300 legal cases related to local elections, Amupitan said, adding that unresolved disputes could complicate its preparations for the forthcoming polls. items.title: South Africa’s Ramaphosa takes AI pitch to Musk's turf
items.author: Tiisetso Motsoeneng
items.summary: The News South African President Cyril Ramaphosa is due to land in California this weekend for a week-long push to court billions in American AI infrastructure investment. The roadshow will throw him into the backyard of Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, whose regulatory clash with Pretoria is at the center of a widening diplomatic rift with Washington. Ramaphosa is likely to face questions about domestic ownership rules which Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has slammed as “openly racist” and cited as the reason his Starlink satellite-internet venture does not operate in Africa’s biggest economy. The working visit , which kicks off on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World summit , unfolds against a deepening diplomatic row as Washington steps up pressure against Pretoria over everything from race policies to its foreign policy choices. South Africa was recently also removed from the African Growth and Opportunity Act preferential trade program. US Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III warned in recent weeks that South Africa’s mandatory local equity ownership transfers under Black Economic Empowerment laws, a policy designed to address dispossessions caused by South Afric

items.title: US commerce secretary in the spotlight over Nvidia scandal
items.author: Prashant Rao
items.summary: US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced mounting pressure from lawmakers over the Trump administration’s handling of the Nvidia scandal. Lutnick has been criticized — including, reportedly, by the Treasury secretary — over his department’s failure to sanction Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, for allegedly smuggling its chips; revelations that a Megaspeed executive, who is accused of ties to Chinese intelligence, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang led to Huang’s downfall. Singapore authorities, meanwhile, said the US provided only “limited” help with the city-state’s investigation into the Megaspeed executive. Multiple Republican senators have called for Lutnick and Huang to appear before the chamber over the still-unfurling episode, while a Republican member of the House told Semafor “ questions need to be answered .” — Prashant Rao

items.title: Trump threatens new tariffs on Mexican goods
items.author: Jeronimo Gonzalez
items.summary: US President Donald Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if it doesn’t stop a migrant caravan heading for the border, ratcheting up tensions with the US’ biggest trading partner. Illegal crossings of the US-Mexico border have plummeted during Trump’s second term partly because Mexico, which sends the vast majority of its exports to its northern neighbor, has deployed troops to stem the flow and win over the White House. The Democratic Party’s recent electoral victories have lifted hopes of a warmer US welcome among would-be migrants. However, Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller — the architect of Washington’s draconian approach to immigration, including divisive raids — to become the president’s chief of staff has dashed hopes of a friendlier policy any time soon. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

items.title: Opinion: STAT+: ‘What will I do with the time I have left?’: What it’s like to find out you might develop Alzheimer’s
items.author: Jason Karlawish
items.summary: This is the second of two pieces about the experiencing of pre-clinical Alzheimer’s. Read the first here . In 1976, at the dawn of the modern Alzheimer’s era, the neurologist Robert Katzman, champion of efforts to extract Alzheimer’s from senility and “normal aging,” concluded his short essay “ The prevalence and malignancy of Alzheimer disease ” with this notably qualified call to action: “In focusing attention on the mortality associated with Alzheimer disease, our goal is not to find a way to prolong the life of severely demented persons, but rather to call attention to our belief that senile as well as presenile forms of Alzheimer are a single disease, a disease whose etiology must be determined, whose course must be aborted, and ultimately a disease to be prevented.” Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: The future of heart drug research in the wake of study setbacks
items.author: Adam Feuerstein and Elaine Chen
items.summary: On this week’s episode of “The Readout LOUD”: the failure of two closely followed heart disease drugs and how these setbacks may impact the future of cardiovascular drug research. Plus, drug safety concerns weigh on some of the biggest companies in the sector. For years, it was widely believed that a deeper understanding of genetics was going to speed the development of newer and better medicines for patients with heart disease. But then came this year’s American Heart Association meeting, which was dominated by presentations of clinical trials that showed no benefit whatsoever for two drugs long thought to be genetically validated. Read the rest...

items.title: 5 takeaways from STAT’s investigation of the sprawling ‘three-parent IVF’ industry
items.author: Megan Molteni
items.summary: The investigation started with a tip from a British couple. After trying to have a second child for several years, they had signed up with a U.S.-based company called International Fertility Group (IFG), paying tens of thousands of dollars for access abroad to an experimental fertility procedure illegal in the U.S. and tightly regulated in the U.K. The procedure, known as MRT — for mitochondrial replacement techniques — is sometimes called “ three-parent IVF ,” because it involves creating embryos that combine the genes of a mother and father with a bit of DNA from the mitochondria of a third person. Read the rest...

items.title: STAT+: Oura’s acquisition of health tech startup raises conflict-of-interest questions for Eli Lilly, experts say
items.author: Elaine Chen
items.summary: Pharma companies that make GLP-1 drugs have increasingly promoted telehealth companies that prescribe the popular treatments. With a new deal announced this week, one of those relationships is expected to grow more complicated. Eli Lilly has been featuring a telehealth company called Counsel Health on a list of providers for patients seeking a GLP-1 prescription. On Tuesday, Counsel said it would be acquired by the smart ring maker Oura , allowing Counsel clinicians access to the data gathered through the ring so they can help customers understand the data and then diagnose or treat any conditions. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: STAT+: Across the U.S., homegrown experiments aim to save kids from their phones
items.author: Isabella Cueto
items.summary: MILWAUKEE — Kat Zilka sat on the floor of her living room, beside a glowing Christmas tree and a pile of essays, and felt like weeping. It was late in 2022, and she had asked her 12th grade digital journalism students to reflect on their relationships to devices. “The things they were writing were deeply disturbing,” she said. Teenagers quietly enduring online abuse, using their phones all night without their parents’ knowledge, or trapped in a cycle of deleting and redownloading social media. Their words made real what Zilka had been observing for years — how the light in students’ eyes was dimmer, especially since Covid — and revealed the astonishing magnitude of the problem. Continue to STAT+ to read the full story...

items.title: Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on restoring trust in science, the state of public health, and RFK Jr.
items.author: Nicholas Florko
items.summary: Abdul El-Sayed will soon become the first epidemiologist in the Senate at a moment that would keep anyone with a public health background up at night. More than 5,000 Americans have been sickened by the measles this year and the United States is expected to lose its formal measles elimination status by the end of the month. Dengue fever is spreading in Florida , respiratory virus season is underway, and the United States just weathered a foodborne illness outbreak that sickened more than 20,000. In a wide-ranging interview with STAT, the Michigan Democrat emphasized that he is hopeful the United States can fix its growing trust-in-science problem, but he expressed frustration — at Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., at drug and insurance companies, and at the field of public health — for leading America down this path. Read the rest...

items.title: The Writer Who Made Food Fun
items.author: Illustration by The Atlantic. Sources: Bettmann / Getty; CSA-Printstock / Getty;
items.summary: Before M. F. K. Fisher picked up her pen, most American food writing had a whiff of Victorian fustiness about it—the pinch of the corset. After Fisher, the genre was set free. With an unerring ear for pitch and tone and a mastery of the short-form essay, Fisher inspired multiple generations of writers who might have otherwise never bothered to think rigorously about how and what we eat, and how food can be a source of physical pleasure. Ruth Reichl, Betty Fussell, the Elizabeth Gilbert of Eat Pray Love —all are Fisher’s children. Picador has recently reissued five classic Fisher collections. To reread them is to grasp not only how much joy she infused into food writing but also how much pain she quietly sublimated into her work. Many gastronomists have followed her example; if only more memoirists did too. Fisher herself didn’t have the benefit of clear antecedents. In the decades before her first essay collection, Serve It Forth , was published in 1937, cookbooks enumerated ways for mothers to keep a household running smoothly—the lineaments of what became known as home economics, with the matriarch as a fastidious field general. items.title: The Shamelessness of Marco Rubio
items.author: Colin Hubbard / AP
items.summary: Next to all of the take-Americans-for-nitwits scams perpetrated by the Trump administration, the news that Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been using taxpayer-funded military jets to fly to college-football games doesn’t amount to that much. Still, as evidence of degraded ethics and an emperor-like feed-me-another-grape sensibility, it holds its own. Rubio has defended his flights by saying that the events are important to his family—his son is a senior running back for the Gators. But he’s really Saturday joyriding to big-ticket events, and the message he’s sending is This administration doesn’t serve you. You serve it. Rubio’s son Anthony may be a very nice young man. What he isn’t, arguably, is a college-football player worth flying in to watch—because he barely ever plays. He is a walk-on, a scout-teamer, which means that his primary role is not to play in games but to be a body for his teammates to scrimmage against during practice. It’s a valuable job, from which he’s no doubt learned a lot. But he has made it onto the field for exactly three rushing attempts this season. items.title: Zelda ’s Midlife Crisis
items.author: Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic
items.summary: M any video games have reached middle age. Pong did in 2012, Space Invaders in 2018, Pac-Man in 2020. Depending on how nerdy you want to get about provenance, Mario turned 40 in 2021 or 2023 or 2025, and Oregon Trail hit the milestone in 2011 or 2025. Video games, a medium for children that has tried and mostly failed to become sophisticated entertainment for adults, are simply old. The Legend of Zelda , which turned 40 this year, is the latest release at the codger arcade. I am, alas, even older than that. My first encounter with Zelda took place at arm’s length. I had seen the strange television ads for the game, because that is how toys and candy were marketed to children. Despite owning a Nintendo Entertainment System, I felt no pull to play or own the game. It seems idiotic to assert that a fantasy-adventure video game with an elfin boy clad in green struck me as childish, but I could already feel adolescence pulling me from Mario to, well, Maria or her equivalent (who was probably named Jennifer or Heather or Michelle). items.title: The Polls Missed the Blue Tsunami. Why Doesn’t Anyone Care?
items.author: Lakshya Jain
items.summary: (Photo illustration by Bill Kuchman/ The Bulwark | Photos: Shutterstock) IN THE WAKE OF THE BLUE TSUNAMI that engulfed America last week, you’ve probably seen some pollsters claiming vindication for the industry. After all, the polls said a blue wave would happen, and it did. The results were proof that, despite the numerous challenges faced by the industry, polling is fine, right? Wrong. I’m not an armchair critic. I am a pollster. Take it from me: The polls did not have a great night. In fact, per data from Matt Grossmann, the director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research at Michigan State University, pollsters may have had one of their worst cycles of this century, with a polling miss exceeding the infamous misfires in 2016 and rivaling those of 2020. The reason it’s not being talked about more is because, in 2026, the misfires went in the opposite direction. The polls this cycle undershot Democrats in fourteen of the fifteen key Senate races—all but Nebraska—and often substantially. items.title: NYC Juvenile Lockups Packed Beyond Capacity as Overtime Soars: Audit
items.author: Reuven Blau
items.summary: The city’s two juvenile detention centers are operating far beyond capacity, staff overtime has quadrupled and the average length of detention has nearly doubled, according to a new state audit. The 69-page review also found that the number of probation officers declined by one-third between 2020 and 2026, even as juvenile caseloads increased. “New York City is spending more money to keep young people in detention, and they are staying there longer,” state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli said in a statement. “The city needs to address staffing shortages and overcrowding and also invest in prevention efforts, including after-school programs, mentoring and summer jobs, to give young people more opportunities and help keep them out of the juvenile justice system.” Overcrowding at the two facilities has gotten so bad the city has been forced to use classroom space as housing units. Earlier this month, a state oversight agency stopped issuing waivers to allow ACS to use those common areas for housing. items.title: The datacenter industry is using propaganda to fight opposition | Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
items.author: Samuel Woolley, Dean Jackson and Maia Woluchem
items.summary: Big tech has used misdirection, disinformation and jargon to obscure the harm the facilities can cause to communities “Antifa”. “Commies”. “Chinese bots”. Everyone from tech leaders to the president has called datacenter resistance a “ documented psyop ” and a “ Chinese PR thing ”. But why do they make these claims? Our new research finds that the datacenter industry uses propaganda, disinformation, and information control to mold public opinion and undermine community opposition.

items.title: Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from USA to Manchester United confirmed
items.author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer and Will Unwin
items.summary: Pochettino to take charge of two final USMNT matches He has signed two-and-a-half-year United contract Mauricio Pochettino’s switch from the US men’s national team to Manchester United has been confirmed. Pochettino will guide the US through a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches on Saturday and Tuesday before joining United, for whom his first game will come at Liverpool next Sunday. The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton manager has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday after leading United to their worst start to a season in four decades. United have won one of their past 11 games and are in the Premier League’s relegation zone.

items.title: What science can tell us about the art of conversation - video
items.author: Ellie Bury, Ian Sample, Joshan Chana, Jacob Liebenberg, Luke John Smith, Madelei
items.summary: Scientists at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire say they have discovered a telltale sign of an enjoyable conversation. Apparently the secret of a mutually satisfying chat is a healthy dose of pink noise. Guardian science editor Ian Sample tells co-host Madeleine Finlay how this concept usually associated with physics can be applied to conversation, and what the secret to pinkifying our chats could be.

items.title: New York is running out of room for its waste even with Statue of Liberty sized landfill
items.author: Oliver Milman
items.summary: One company is proposing elongating the life of the dump, pungent smell and all, several more decades As a visual representation of how New York is running out of places to put its waste, the largest active landfill in the state is a striking one. The hulking Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty and its operators are seeking to raise it even further, to the consternation of nearby residents. The landfill, situated in the scenic Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state, has grown since the 1980s to now sprawl across 350 acres of deposited trash, mounded up to the height of around 300ft – roughly the same height of the Statue of Liberty.

items.title: Iran says it targeted US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike

items.title: Democrats made shocking gains with religious voters — but not everywhere
items.author: Christian Paz
items.summary: Voters arrive to cast their ballots at a polling location inside St. Patrick Parish Center in White Lake, Michigan on Election Day. | Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images One of the most eye-opening aspects of last week’s midterms was the new cohort of religious politicians it sent to Congress — many of them part of a wave of Democratic-leaning Christians . Another striking feature was the dramatic shift among many religious voters. For years, American politics has seemed stuck on a partisan track, with religious-identified voters shifting more firmly to the right, and the nonreligious tacking to the left. There are a few exceptions , of course — Jewish voters, Latino Catholics, and Black Protestants, who have stayed firmly Democratic — but the broader tide has flowed clearly one way. Key takeaways This year’s blue tsunami carried voters everywhere to the left; it also scrambled voting trends in America’s religious electorate. Catholics shifted hard to the left after Donald Trump won their vote by a double-digit margin in 2024. items.title: Why online gamblers are obsessed with table tennis
items.author: Jack Meserve
items.summary: If you were living in Colorado in May and bet on sports online, you’d statistically have been most likely to bet on professional basketball. Next on the list was baseball. The third-most wagered sport? Table tennis. Colorado is almost certainly not an outlier. Table tennis occupies a similarly high ranking in Oregon , the only other state to provide sport-by-sport breakdowns of gambling revenue. And it’s likely true in every other state that allows sports gambling. This is a strange fact, one that’s been reported by a few local and national outlets. And beyond the bets involved, it’s also a window into where sports gambling is going, and how sports betting is morphing into something stranger and more destructive than dropping $100 on the New York Yankees to cover the spread on Saturday. There’s the old quip that the Holy Roman Empire was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. In some sense, this is sports betting that involves neither sports nor betting. The gambling on table tennis isn’t really on the game of table tennis. It’s on a strange simulacrum of table tennis created solely for the purpose of creating more ways to gamble on it. items.summary: Since bursting on the scene two years ago, prediction markets have become one of the buzziest new sectors in finance, pulling in billions of dollars in revenue, and driving daily news headlines. The young industry is dominated by two giants, Kalshi and Polymarket, but numerous other companies are trying to muscle into the field. That includes the sports-focused prediction market Novig, which only launched as a federally regulated prediction market in August, but has already claimed the number three spot by one widely used industry metric. Over the past 30 days, Novig handled $1.8 billion in trading volume on U.S.-regulated exchanges, according to the PM Pulse, a newsletter that tracks prediction market volume using data from research firm Aldrin. That figure is small next to Kalshi’s $33.3 billion and Polymarket U.S.’s $6.3 billion. But it’s about $300 million ahead of Crypto.com, the fourth-place contender, and its volume is up 80% from the previous 30 days. The volume figures don’t account for combos, or multi-game parlays, which Sam Schwartz, who runs the newsletter, says can inflate volume without producing proportionally more revenue for the exchange. Well, at least the idea of Nashville, the country music mecca that is perpetually struggling to define itself within and against the country at large, a place that has always been more diverse than its reputation yet still stands for a certain image of white, Christian Americana. items.title: ‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul
items.author: Lanre Bakare
items.summary: After wittily blending pop and politics on their debut, the Belgians are now processing their personal lives. Zeebroek is encouraging his bandmate Charlotte Adigéry and I to crane our necks towards the Mammelokker, an 18th-century Flemish relief on the top of the building. It’s a gruesome bit of stone, which sits above the town square and depicts a daughter suckling her own father. The pair are taking me on a tour of their medieval home town, and this disturbing architectural decoration is part of our itinerary.

items.summary: (Erased Tapes) Dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements, virtuosic vocals and echoes of PJ Harvey and Massive Attack make this disarming debut a one-of-a-kind creation Since the release of her debut EP, Qasr , in 2024, south Asian-American vocalist and composer Sheherazaad has developed a distinctive take on the classical singing of her heritage. While her contemporaries such as the singers Ganavya and Manizeh draw on spiritual vocal traditions, and Arooj Aftab on jazz and folk instrumentation, Sheherazaad’s work is darker and far more introspective, using sparse acoustic arrangements to create a style of Urdu-language noir. On this debut album, she delivers her most disarmingly eerie and mournful work yet. A heavy layer of reverb coats the record’s spare and often evocative arrangements, making undulating tabla hits echo beneath Sheherazaad’s keening vocals on Qatil, while on Registaan it lends an unnervingly distorted quality to a simple guitar refrain and on Mard it subsumes melody in a haze of resonance. items.summary: (Stem) Her truly remarkable, Sade-ish voice is hypnotic against some dizzyingly plush production, but a modern spin on 80s pastiche sometimes veers too close to tribute Swedish-Iranian singer Snoh Aalegra has previously described her music – a lush, pastiche-y mix of R&B, hip-hop, soul and pop – as “cinematic soul”. But although she’s a dab hand at graceful, timeless presentation (and has a truly remarkable voice) Aalegra’s music has often struggled to match up to its aesthetic, hampered by her love of the greats and a penchant for broadly generic lyrics. Her most recent album, 2021’s Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies , made some headway toward carving out a more distinctive sound, thanks to sparky and inventive production from Tyler, the Creator, No ID, P2J and the Neptunes, but still didn’t quite feel like the right fit. Aalegra’s fourth album is her most successful front-to-back statement yet, even if she can’t shake off the talent-show-ish reverence for her idols. Flávio Bolsonaro, Viktor Orbán, Reform UK, the Tories and a vast array of Republican candidates have all been rejected in national or local contests this year, even in usually reliably conservative Mississippi. Apparently impregnable incumbents and populist insurgents alike have been beaten, often by big margins . Texas elected its first Democratic senator since 1988 and its first Latina governor , while Democrats won governorships in all four southern border states and every southern border congressional district. The summit’s co-hosts are now trying to get countries to promise to increase their electricity use to 35% of all energy used by 2035. items.title: Perceiving greater discrimination in health care, the LGBTQIA+ community delays seeking medical appointments
items.summary: People in the LGBTQ+ community face extra barriers in their daily lives due to their sexual orientation or gender identity. One of the areas where these individuals sometimes suffer discrimination is in health care. In fact, a survey by the State Federation of Lesbians, Gays, Trans, Bisexual, and Intersex People found that more than 20% of the trans people surveyed had felt discriminated against when visiting primary care providers.

items.title: Young Australians are paying the price for a health system that doesn't fit their lives

Nearly one in three have taken time off work, study or caregiving responsibilities to see a GP, while one in five delayed care because of cost in the past 12 months.

items.title: The moon is not the Wild West: Experts call for a pause on lunar industrialization
items.author: Ingrida Kuzborskaja
items.summary: As the major powers and the private companies go full tilt with their plans to develop infrastructure and extract resources on the moon, the questions around environmental protection, international regulation and who benefits all come into play. Vilnius University Institute of International Relations and Political Science (VU IIRPS) professor Florian Rabitz, together with Xiao-Shan Yap from Utrecht University, explores these concerns in their research article, "Don't Fly Me to the Moon: A Moratorium on Lunar Industrialization," published in the journal Global Environmental Politics.

Van Hollen (D-Md.) has served in the Senate since 2017 and has been in Congress since 2003. Schumer has been the Senate Democratic leader since 2017 and has served in the Senate since 1999. Driving the news: "In this election, the American people called for change," Van Hollen said in a statement on Thursday. "They called for a change from Donald Trump's disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn't working for working people." "It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. items.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
items.summary: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.

items.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
items.summary: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.

items.title: Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why
items.summary: Colorectal cancer is making an alarming comeback in the United States after more than 20 years of declining rates, and the increase is no longer limited to younger adults. A major new study found rising rates across nearly every age group under 70, including older Americans who have historically benefited most from cancer screening.

items.title: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that where men get their protein may be linked to their testosterone levels. Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.

items.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
items.summary: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

items.title: A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy
items.summary: Researchers at Brown University have overcome a major obstacle to creating ultra-low-power computer chips that could help slash the energy demands of AI. Their breakthrough eliminates a long-standing "dead layer" problem that causes promising materials to stop working when made extremely thin.

items.title: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
items.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.

items.title: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a surprising hidden function of a protein that may hold the key to repairing damaged muscles and treating muscular dystrophy. Known for protecting chromosomes, TRF2 also helps muscle stem cells maintain their identity and regenerate injured tissue. When scientists removed the protein in mice, muscles struggled to repair themselves, and muscular dystrophy progressed dramatically faster.

items.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
items.summary: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

items.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
items.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.

Yet far more scandalous than Huang’s affair(s) is the apparent coverup by a Trump administration so keen to protect its friends, and so eager to juice the stock market, that it was willing to trade away U.S. interests. Put another way, the horndog may be the headline. But the real story is the transactional way the Trump administration handles all of America’s economic security. This is one of the biggest national security scandals in decades. It also could cause serious economic damage, as it undermines our domestic AI industry and boosts China’s. Heads. Should. Roll. items.title: Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart handed 3-game ban after swinging at Warriors center Charles Bassey
items.summary: A late-game punch just cost Marcus Smart three games. The NBA suspended the Houston Rockets guard without pay on Thursday after swinging at, then grazing, Golden State Warriors center Charles Bassey. Doing the exact opposite of his last name, the 32-year-old former Defensive Player of the Year melted down in the third quarter of Houston's 115-108 win. Smart and Bassey got tied up fighting for position under the glass, barked at each other trailing the play, and Smart uncorked a right hook that grazed Bassey's nose. items.summary: In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test. Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday. Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years. items.title: Ancient climate records reveal how East Asian monsoon shifted abruptly into cold and drought

Researchers from Utrecht University's Faculty of Geosciences, together with colleagues at research institutes in China and Belgium, are investigating this question by looking back 250,000 years. They found that, over long timescales, the monsoon system tracks changes in incoming solar radiation caused by variations in Earth's orbit and tilt. But when radiation falls below a certain threshold, abrupt periods of extreme cold and drought occur, particularly when atmospheric CO₂ concentrations are low. The study was published in Communications Earth & Environment.

items.title: Investigating Michel Houellebecq Is a Dangerous Mistake
items.author: Benjamin de Diesbach / Hans Lucas / AFP / Getty
items.summary: An assault on free speech is unfolding in France. On Tuesday, a judge placed Michel Houellebecq, one of the country’s most significant living writers, under investigation for his alleged “complicity in incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence,” an accusation that stems from comments he made about Muslims several years ago. Houellebecq’s remarks were controversial and insensitive, but defending his freedom to speak does not require finding his words unobjectionable. Even the most offensive generalizations about minority groups should have to meet an exceptionally high threshold to warrant such a legal intervention. Houellebecq’s do not. The fact that he now faces the possibility of criminal charges should concern anyone who professes to care about the free exchange of ideas. Jensen Huang was not just the CEO of the world’s most important semiconductor company. He was also one of Donald Trump’s closest and most influential advisers on AI. Huang persuaded Trump to abandon his initial embrace of export controls, arguing that U.S. technology firms should compete in China. He persistently argued that AI is more akin to electricity than a weapon and that warnings about AI safety were wildly overblown—a view that Trump fully internalized. In the coming months, Congress will scrutinize every aspect of the scandal. Among these are the Commerce Department’s suspension of its investigation into Megaspeed, the Singaporean company that Alice Huang was a director of; the failure to crack down on China’s extensive chip-smuggling operation in Southeast Asia; Nvidia’s financial contributions to Trump’s pet projects, such as the White House ballroom; and China’s possible illicit influence over other business leaders in America

items.title: How a warming ocean is changing the base of the marine food web
items.summary: Climate change is causing warming in the oceans, which can have significant effects on marine food webs. Rising ocean temperatures can intensify seawater stratification, a process in which ocean water forms layers of different densities that mix less readily. This can reduce the supply of nutrients to surface waters and favor smaller phytoplankton species that are better adapted to low-nutrient conditions. Phytoplankton support zooplankton, which in turn transfer energy to fish and other animals. Changes in phytoplankton communities can therefore lead to cascading effects on marine food webs.

(ABC) and The Times of London. Shortly after departure, however, a sudden storm pushed the 20-foot skiff off course, leaving it stranded in open waters . items.author: Marina Bolotnikova
items.summary: This story is part of a series supported by Animal Charity Evaluators, which received a grant from EarthShare. Deep-blue, regulation-happy California is not usually imagined as factory farm country. But the state leads the US in agricultural output, and it is, by a wide margin, America’s top producer of dairy, one of the most brutal sectors in our food system. And it turns out that one of the most foundational, most disturbing practices found in modern dairy farming may already be illegal under a California animal cruelty law — but state officials have shown little inclination to look into it. At any given time, 9 million to 10 million dairy cows populate farms across the US, and California is home to 1.7 million of them, the vast majority of whom are raised on mega dairies . Because cows, like other mammals, must give birth to produce milk, dairy farming is organized around continuous cycles of pregnancy, birth, and lactation. Dairy cows typically give birth around once a year; their calves are then promptly taken from them. Depending on their sex, the calves will eventually join a milking herd or be raised for beef. items.title: A New Pill Could Reduce the Risk of Having a Second Stroke
items.author: Alice Park
items.summary: —utah778—Getty Images On November 9, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a new type of medication to reduce the risk of strokes in certain populations. Asundexian, which will be sold under the brand name Sunharbo, is a daily pill that is the first to target a specific factor in the blood-clotting process that can contribute to stroke. In a study submitted to the FDA by Bayer, researchers found that the drug, when combined with an antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin, reduced the risk of an additional stroke by 26% in just over a year compared to people who received placebo and the antiplatelet therapy. The drug is approved for people who have recently had an ischemic stroke, which occur when clots block blood flow to the brain, or a transient ischemic attack caused by a temporary blockage of blood flow to the brain that doesn’t cause permanent damage. “The data is quite robust, and the feedback from the international stroke community is positive,” says Dr. Ashkan Shoamanesh, professor of medicine at McMaster University, who co-led the trial. “We’re eager to have this on hand as soon as possible for patients.” There are two types of strokes: ischemic strokes, caused

items.title: Hospital sewers may be breeding grounds for dangerous superbugs, study finds
items.summary: Hospital wastewater has been shown to promote the growth of antibiotic-resistant bacteria , potentially making sewer systems hotspots for antimicrobial resistance, according to a new Swedish study published in Nature Communications. Antibiotics taken by patients can pass through their bodies and enter hospital sewer systems, creating conditions that favor the growth of resistant bacteria. Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive drugs designed to kill them, making some infections harder to treat. More than 9.3 million drug-resistant infections occur in the U.S. each year, resulting in more than 39,000 deaths, according to the CDC's 2026 Antimicrobial Resistance Threats Report. They wanted to determine whether hospital wastewater actually promoted the growth of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, rather than simply carrying resistant bacteria from patients. Kane, a longtime Patriots fan, recently became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d’Or, soccer’s award for the best player in the world. The 33-year-old England captain this month signed a contract extension to stay at Bayern until 2029, so it’s unclear when he’d be ready to give NFL kicking a shot. Kane has mused over the years about trying it. He has even floated the idea of combining his NFL dream with joining a Major League Soccer team. "I think I’ve seen him maybe kick a few, and he looked pretty good," Maye said. "No doubt, he does that for a living, so I’m sure he’d be just fine." With Google's recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company's products. Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it's 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces "fabricated claims" by more than 5x, according to Google's analysis. items.title: The Guardian view on Gaza’s misery: don’t let Palestinian deaths mount in this bleak winter | Editorial
items.author: Editorial
items.summary: The formation of a new Israeli government won’t stop the killing, but sustained international pressure must be applied What do you call a ceasefire when the firing has not ceased? The killings in Gaza decreased when the truce was announced last October, but they did not end. Israel’s strike on Thursday morning on one of the few remaining functioning hospitals , which killed six people and wounded 28 more, was the first on a healthcare facility since then. But it was not an anomaly. About four Palestinians a day have died on average since the ceasefire was declared. The Israeli military said that it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters in the attack on Nasser hospital, without providing evidence. Its record does not inspire confidence in the accuracy of its account. Multiple UN experts and health campaigners have warned of the deliberate targeting of medical facilities and healthcare workers. Israeli military personnel have also described the shockingly high level of civilian deaths tolerated as “collateral damage” in targeting even low-level fighters after the brutal Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023.

items.title: The Guardian view on venture capitalism: investor profits are no industrial strategy | Editorial
items.author: Editorial
items.summary: Higher returns for backers do not guarantee national prosperity. Public investment should develop domestic capabilities and meet urgent social needs Britain keeps selling its most valuable companies. The Financial Times calculates that 300 went to foreign buyers, mostly American, over the past decade. What if innovation were scaled up to serve social needs here rather than US investors’ profits? That is the provocation issued by the thinktank Common Wealth in a paper titled We Aren’t the Champions, which takes aim at the UK’s venture capital (VC) industry. The authors say that as long as the UK is subordinated to US cash, getting startups to a heavyweight size will be a sisyphean task . Britain’s tech pioneers are often sold before they become giants. DeepMind, founded in London in 2010, went to Google just four years later. Britain’s venture capitalists might argue that they are in it for themselves, not for building up British tech.

As previously reported , Bird has directed some of our all-time favorite animated films: The Iron Giant (1999), The Incredibles (2004), and Ratatouille (2007), with the latter two snagging well-deserved Oscar wins. He's been kicking around the idea for Ray Gunn for the last 30 years, working on his many other film projects while the Ray Gunn script—co-written by Matthew Robbins, who also co-wrote 1987’s Batteries Not Included with Bird—“stayed in a filing cabinet at Warner Brothers,” the director said earlier this year. The film’s inspiration came when Bird heard the opening of the B-52s’ “ Planet Claire ” (a personal favorite that also provides the soundtrack to the new trailer) and initially thought it was a cover of Henry Mancini’s theme music from the classic TV show Peter Gunn .
