Every other Apple Silicon Mac has found a way to move forward over the last half-decade—we've gotten a more Pro design for the MacBook Pro, a mini-er design for the Mac mini, and a Mac Studio that has finally made Apple admit it doesn't want to make the Mac Pro anymore. Now, Google is ready to take another swing at " intelligent eyewear " for the Gemini era after previewing its plans a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they're no impulse buy. These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered. Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. items.title: Man's secret use of synthetic testosterone for cows nearly destroyed his heart
items.author: Beth Mole
items.summary: For 11 years, a Massachusetts man had an alarming array of health problems, most notably that his heart kept failing. He landed in the hospital over and over again, needed life support at one point, spent years going to specialists, and underwent a barrage of tests along the way. But through it all, he never revealed a key detail behind his ailments: He was taking powerful, illicit synthetic testosterone derivatives (aka anabolic-androgenic steroids, or AAS). One of the drugs he took was approved only for use in animals; it's primarily used to beef up cows. Left in the dark, his doctors had to puzzle this out on their own. In a case report in this week's issue of the New England Journal of Medicine, they explain how they did it. They also offer a warning: These cases will only become more common, and clinicians need to know what they look like. Read full article Comments

items.title: The amazing disappearing exoplanet
items.author: John Timmer
items.summary: One nice thing about discovering exoplanets is that, once you work out how long their orbits take, they continue to show up like clockwork. The timing is so regular, in fact, that we can use variations to detect the gravitational influence of additional planets in the same exosolar system. And the precise timing is useful in that we can rely on it to point telescopes at the system when we know some of the light we detect has passed through the planet's atmosphere. Except when we can't. On Monday, researchers reported on an exoplanet that simply stopped showing up. TOI-2535b is a hot Jupiter-sized planet we've been observing as it transits between its host star, TOI-2535, and Earth for about seven years now. But it recently stopped showing up, and researchers suspect that's due to an unseen companion orbiting in a different plane. Read full article Comments

items.title: Building a rocket is hard. AST SpaceMobile thinks it's "simple."
items.author: Eric Berger
items.summary: During an hour-long event on Thursday, Abel Avellan, the founder and chief executive of the telecommunications company AST SpaceMobile, laid out his vision for developing a large rocket to launch his Bluebird satellites into orbit. Avellan emphasized, over and over again, that AST plans to build a "simple" rocket. He paraphrased SpaceX founder Elon Musk several times, saying, "the best part is no part." Avellan emphasized that AST has already procured engines for its proposed Blacklift rocket, asserting that engine development accounts for 80 percent of a typical rocket's development cycle. "Of course rocket engineers are going to get mad with me, but you can simplify it as a big tank feeding engines," he said of the rocket. "So big tanks—we know how to do them. We know how to do them. We know how to do them in composite." Read full article Comments

items.title: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
items.author: Ashley Belanger
items.summary: CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI. The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried. In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!” Read full article Comments

items.title: T-Mobile illegally imposed 50GB cap on low-income home Internet plan, NY says
items.author: Jon Brodkin
items.summary: T-Mobile violated a New York state law by imposing a 50GB-per-month data cap and reducing speeds to less than a megabit per second on home Internet plans it is required to offer people with low incomes, New York government officials alleged. T-Mobile agreed to a settlement requiring it to scrap the data and speed limits, to offer the required low-income plans to more parts of the state, and to make it easier for customers to find information about the plans. The settlement requires T-Mobile to eliminate the speed limits and expand availability of the plans within 120 days. The alleged legal violation and the settlement are related to T-Mobile's wireless home Internet service, not the company's mobile plans. Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the settlement on Monday, saying that a state investigation found T-Mobile violated the New York Affordable Broadband Act (ABA). At that point, Nvidia sported the world’s biggest market cap at $5.85 trillion. Wall Street analysts following the stock were almost universal even then in acclaiming Nvidia as a cheap stock. Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of affairs with a direct report and with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy , yet the national security questions he leaves behind keep growing amidst escalating congressional investigations . Neither Nvidia nor Powell has publicly addressed that report. CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO , and one of her first moves was addressing employees. items.author: Michaela Herbst
items.summary: The CEO of British multinational bank Standard Chartered says “geopolitical fragmentation is an advantage for us,” after the lender reported a 46% jump in third-quarter net profit to $1.5 billion. Speaking at a media roundtable, Bill Winters said the splintering of global trade is creating new business for the bank, which helps multinational corporations manage cross-border deals, the South China Morning Post reported . His remarks come as companies rethink where they make things amid rising trade tensions. Many have adopted a “China plus one” strategy, shifting some production to Southeast Asia to offset China’s rising costs. That shift has proven more complicated than expected, as many factories in the region still rely on Chinese inputs, Fortune reported in October . Why a fractured economy is good business for Standard Chartered Geopolitical fragmentation refers to the structural shift in the global economy as supply chains, trade, and policy realign along political lines. For banks, that shift changes where money flows. items.title: ‘The plot twist’: A study of 73,000 adults found America’s richest still die sooner than most Europeans
items.author: Lena Borrelli
items.summary: Americans have never earned more or lived longer. Median household income hit $87,460 in 2025, the highest since the Census Bureau began tracking it in 1967, according to Census data released in September . Life expectancy reached 79 years in 2024, also a record . Yet money still can’t buy Americans a European lifespan. A Brown University study published last year in the New England Journal of Medicine found that Americans die sooner than Europeans at every level of wealth, and that the richest Americans fare no better than the poorest people in much of Western Europe. “The plot twist is that even the wealthiest quartile of Americans does not have better outcomes than most of northern and Western Europeans,” says Sara Machado, a research scientist at Brown’s Center for Health System Sustainability. “That was unexpected and counters a lot of the narrative that we’re used to.” What the Brown study found The researchers tracked more than 73,000 adults ages 50 to 85 in the U.S. and 16 European countries, starting in 2010 and following them for about a decade, using data from the U.S. Health and Retirement Study and Europe’s SHARE survey. items.title: AI used to better predict kidney stone composition
items.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers developed and tested an artificial intelligence (AI) model that used results from a standard 24-hour urine test to predict kidney stone composition more accurately than a conventional urine-based calculation. Using the AI model, researchers correctly predicted kidney stone composition in 73% of patients, compared with 33% using the conventional calculation alone.

items.title: American Cancer Society updates prostate cancer screening guideline: Regular PSA testing for average- and high-risk men
items.summary: The American Cancer Society (ACS) today released an updated guideline for prostate cancer screening to help find cancer before it spreads and reduce the risk of dying from the disease. Key changes include a direct recommendation for prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based screening every two years for average-risk men aged 50–69, with clinicians ensuring patients understand the potential benefits, limitations and harms before starting screening. Also, ACS recommends annual PSA-based screening beginning at 45 years old for Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer.

items.title: Cell changes around early breast cancers provide clues to why some cases become invasive
items.summary: Researchers at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have created one of the most detailed maps to date of the cell environment surrounding ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), the most common form of preinvasive, or stage 0, breast cancer. The findings may help explain why some lesions progress to invasive breast cancer and others do not, informing strategies to improve patient risk prediction and develop better targeted approaches for patients at higher risk of invasive disease.

items.title: Inflammation is involved in the earliest stages of atherosclerosis
items.summary: Inflammation plays an important role in the development of atherosclerosis from its earliest stages, long before the onset of symptoms or cardiovascular events such as heart attack or stroke. This is the main conclusion of a study led by a team at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC) and published in the European Heart Journal. The research shows that systemic inflammation contributes to disease development independently of traditional cardiovascular risk factors such as elevated cholesterol and hypertension.

items.title: Euclid offers best-ever 3D map of the universe to date
items.summary: The Euclid Consortium and the European Space Agency (ESA) have released the first major batch of data from the Euclid space telescope. This release, which captures light from more than a billion objects and covers an area of sky equivalent to 9,500 full moons, lays the foundation for Europe's dark universe detective's largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos. Several German research facilities play crucial roles in the Euclid mission's success.

items.title: Unified framework establishes rules for classifying unconventional magnets
items.summary: Researchers from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science (HFIPS) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) have developed a unified framework for establishing symmetry criteria and classifying unconventional magnets.

items.title: High water, high rents: Poorest residents pay the most for climate adaptation
items.summary: As cities worldwide adapt to extreme weather, climate adaptation must prevent people from wading through flooded streets in the future. But the costs are not equally shared. A study from the University of Copenhagen shows that climate adaptation policies may even make social inequality worse. In Copenhagen, stormwater costs fall disproportionately on not-for-profit housing residents, as these neighborhoods are often located near climate adaptation projects.

items.title: How human ideas evolve: Technical progress may not require weeding out weaker designs
items.summary: Human culture evolves similarly to living organisms, but unlike biology, human creativity can accumulate improvements at an incredible speed. But how exactly does the process of transmitting and modifying ideas between people work?

items.title: Large mutation analysis challenges claim that evolution shields important genes from changes
items.summary: The idea that important genes mutate less frequently than others was first proposed in 1972 as a challenge to the traditional view of evolution. But the claim has remained contentious. Now, new research from the University of Bath finds the evidence behind that theory to be flawed.

items.title: Lipids from banana peels help cherry tomatoes stay fresh longer
items.summary: Fruits and vegetables keep "breathing" even after they're picked. Respiration consumes sugars and organic acids that contribute to flavor, while moisture loss and continued ripening soften the fruit. These changes shorten shelf life and contribute to food waste. Thin edible coatings can be applied to regulate gas and water transfer and preserve fresh produce. Now, food scientists are exploring whether byproducts we often discard could supply ingredients for these coatings.

items.title: A new twist on 'magic-angle' graphene: Tuning resistance with strain
items.summary: In materials science labs around the world, researchers regularly reproduce a peculiar experiment. Under a microscope, they use tiny robotic manipulators to lay two sheets of carbon, each a single atom thick, against one another. They then rotate the top sheet against the bottom. The two identical lattices of atoms, when twisted relative to one another, bloom into a complex moiré pattern, a shifting complex of honeycomb shapes that grow and shrink as the angle between the layers changes.

items.title: Study finds midlife women face unique need for workplace flexibility
items.summary: New research from the Working for Women Research Partnership (WFWRP) shows overlapping life demands make women ages 40–55 more likely than other groups to both want and need workplace flexibility.

items.title: Nitrate pollution in rivers linked to dry climates, not just human activity
items.summary: Nitrate, a chemical compound of oxygen and nitrogen often used in farm fertilizers, can rise to toxic levels in surrounding water under very dry conditions. This relationship has traditionally been attributed to agricultural runoff or human waste in the environment, but new research led by scientists at Penn State shows that a hot and dry climate elevates concentrations of nitrate in rivers and streams, even in areas without urban or agricultural development.

items.title: Rain may increase ocean carbon uptake more than we thought
items.summary: Global carbon budgets, which track carbon's movement among the atmosphere, ocean and land, may underestimate how much carbon the ocean absorbs by roughly 5% to 15% because current estimates do not fully account for rain's effects on the ocean surface.

items.title: Feeling pressured to be grateful? Don't force it
items.summary: It's that time of year when gratitude seems to be everywhere: at work, around the dinner table and at holiday gatherings. But with so much pressure to feel thankful, gratitude can start to feel like one more thing on the holiday to-do list.

items.title: Finding romance with AI: Study explores benefits, limits of chatbot intimacy
items.author: Noor Hindi
items.summary: An AI companion can be available for a late-night conversation, respond to personal disclosures and discuss a favorite topic for hours. For people who develop intimate relationships with chatbots, those exchanges can offer a meaningful sense of connection.

items.title: Seaweeds can switch to asexual reproduction when there are no mates nearby
items.summary: Kelp switch between sexual and asexual reproduction depending on whether there are potential mates nearby, according to a study by Daniel Liesner at the Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Germany, and colleagues, published Nov. 12 in the open-access journal PLOS Biology.

items.title: Sensors track stress in plants in real time—without hurting them in the process
items.summary: Even plants, from towering palm trees to vegetables such as onions and eggplants, can get stressed. Now, a team of engineers has designed a new kind of sensor that attaches directly to plants and peers inside them to track how they respond to stressors such as drought and fires in real time.

items.title: Sequential peaks in arthropod availability across snow and vegetation help sustain alpine birds
items.summary: The alpine zone is located above the tree line in mountainous regions and is characterized by long winters and short growing seasons. Birds and other animals inhabiting these environments breed during a limited period extending from spring to summer. Arthropods, including insects and spiders, serve as an essential food resource during this time.

items.title: Space dust particles point to ancient heavy-oxygen water reservoir in the Kuiper belt
items.summary: Way out past the asteroid belt, another belt encircles the planets in our solar system. The Kuiper belt, beyond Neptune, preserves icy bodies that escaped much of the processing experienced by objects closer to the sun. Unlike the rocky and metallic asteroid belt, Kuiper belt objects are composed mostly of frozen water, methane and ammonia, mixed with rock and dust.

items.title: Tiny cracks and a 9-volt battery could help fight deadly superbugs
items.summary: As superbugs become harder to treat and antibiotic resistance continues to rise worldwide, Flinders University scientists have uncovered an unlikely ally in the fight to prevent infections before they take hold. They have found that carefully controlled microscopic cracks can enhance the performance of an antibacterial coating, which helps destroy dangerous bacteria when activated with a small electrical charge.

items.title: More Than Numbers: Portraits of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
items.author: Sarahbeth Maney
items.summary: The Department of Homeland Security says it’s not detaining Americans. In written statements, it has said that “allegations that ICE is arresting and deporting U.S. citizens is FALSE.” It has said that “when individuals are briefly questioned under ‘reasonable suspicion’ and are found to be U.S. citizens, they are immediately released.” And it has said that “U.S. citizen agitators are only held while they actively remain a safety threat to our officers and the public.” But ProPublica has identified more than 500 citizens detained since President Donald Trump returned to office. They are not just numbers. Among them is an elderly car wash owner whom agents repeatedly knocked to the ground as they detained several of his workers. A 6-year-old whose mother says still has nightmares after agents pointed guns at him and his siblings. A high school senior who was detained after she tried to stop officers from questioning her autistic younger brother. A dad who was held for several days and missed his daughter’s third birthday. And many Democrats — fresh off an electoral rout of the GOP — are spoiling for a fight. “I want Pete Hegseth not just impeached, I want him prosecuted. They murdered people in the Caribbean. And we killed 163 little girls in Iran,” Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., told The Intercept on Tuesday. “Everybody in my class is ready for him to go. We tried it. It didn’t work. We’ll do it again.” A mountain of evidence is poised to fall on Hegseth’s head. He could be convicted of countless crimes. But just because Congress has a government official dead to rights doesn’t mean that that official won’t evade justice. The Russian comedy duo known as Vovan and Lexus have pulled off a long string of prank telephone calls to famous figures since 2011, with victims ranging from Elton John to John McCain. The group, whose pranks have often aligned with Russian foreign policy priorities, have been accused of working in league with its government , a charge they deny. items.title: New Trump Rule Threatens Immigrant Families With Separation or Homelessness
items.author: Jessica Washington
items.summary: The Trump administration is preparing to kick nearly 80,000 people, about half of them children, off federal housing assistance over their family’s immigration status, threatening to drive thousands into homelessness. On Thursday, the Department of Housing and Urban Development published a final rule that’s on track to effectively bar families of mixed immigration status from receiving most federal housing assistance, which allow people to receive housing vouchers to reside in privately owned rental homes or in government-owned or -assisted public housing units. As it stands, undocumented immigrants and temporary non-residents in the United States already are barred from personally receiving most forms of federal housing assistance. But if some members of the family are eligible, the eligible members can receive prorated assistance to help cover their housing, and the non-eligible family member can live with them. The new rule, which goes into effect in mid-December, would disqualify an entire family if one member is ineligible after a temporary grace period, forcing them to choose between separation and eviction. items.title: The True Story Behind Get Huge and a Series of Unexplained Deaths Linked to Looksmaxxing
items.author: Barry Levitt
items.summary: Tony Huge in the docuseries Get Huge —Courtesy of Hulu “A day natty is a day wasted.” That’s the motto of Tony Huge, a prominent figure in the looksmaxxing community. In Huge’s lingo, “natty” means “natural,” as in refraining from using a heavy regimen of supplements popular in the rapidly growing online subculture of men that promotes extreme measures to maximize the potential of one’s physical appearance. Especially popular among young adults and teenagers, looksmaxxing often includes risky behavior like the use of trenbolone, a steroid designed to promote muscle growth in livestock that’s illegal for human use in the United States, and DNP, a toxic fertilizer that can burn fat but brings the potential for deadly side effects. For looksmaxxers, the goal is to achieve peak physical form to become more powerful and attractive to women—life expectancy be damned. Filmmaker Stacey Lee first met Huge in late 2024, when looksmaxxing was still “a very fringe movement.” She was embarking on a project about the phenomenon, which she says has moved “to center stage” between then and the Nov. 10 release of her three-part series Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death , streaming on Hulu and Disney+.

Phishing emails resemble legitimate messages and are designed to spoof recipients into giving up personal data. “I was wondering, as a sleep researcher, what sleep would do to that,” he says. items.title: The Next Chapter of mRNA
items.author: Alice Park
items.summary: It’s been a very good year for Stéphane Bancel. On a crisp October day, the CEO of Moderna, of COVID-vaccine fame, is sitting in his glass-walled office in the company’s headquarters in Cambridge, Mass., weeks before encouraging results from the company’s first mRNA cancer vaccine would become public. He’s recounting the biotech’s rocky road turning an unproven, scientifically dismissed approach—using messenger RNA, or mRNA, the genetic code that instructs cells to make proteins—into a platform for producing new categories of medicines. Fifteen years ago, Bancel had his doubts. At the time, there were no approved mRNA-based products on the market, and most scientists would have agreed that mRNA was too unstable to form the basis of a new class of medical treatments. In fact, the entire biotech industry had bet—successfully—on manipulating another, more reliable genetic material: DNA. “It was crazy to think of using mRNA as a drug,” Bancel reflects. But that was before a fateful meeting forced him to look at the genetic material in a different way, and realize that with the right manipulation, mRNA provided a way to make drugs that were never possible with existing strategies. items.title: The Toxic Vengeance of Capital Punishment
items.author: Dominic Erdozain
items.summary: —Max Zolotukhin—Getty Images Two radical ideas have been introduced into human thought, wrote the novelist and humorist Kurt Vonnegut. One was that “energy and matter are pretty much the same sort of stuff.” That was Einstein. The other was that “revenge is a bad idea.” That was Jesus. We are so wired for vengeance, so trained to retaliate, mused Vonnegut, Jesus must be classed among the revolutionaries. Vonnegut was no Christian, preferring to describe himself as a “Christ-worshipping agnostic,” but he dreamed of a world in which the long “chain of death and destruction” is broken. That is why he opposed the death penalty and one of the reasons he despaired of America. News that the execution of former Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan , who murdered 13 U.S. soldiers in 2009, will not be livestreamed in December has been well received, but reports that a narrow majority of Americans approve of both the sentence and the method of death-by-firing-squad have excited little comment. Coming days after the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, for a crime committed when she was a teenager, it is reasonable to ask: Why do we still execute people? items.title: When accessible voting isn’t accessible: A blind voter’s experience at the polls
items.author: Baylee Alger / Wisconsin Watch
items.summary: Reading Time: 2 minutes Shortly before the election I wrote about the barriers to voting I face as someone who is blind. I described how, at almost 27 years old, I had never voted because I worried about a lack of privacy in the process. Traditional ways of voting would require me to get someone else’s help — whether checking boxes on a paper ballot or choosing a candidate on a screen. But while reporting the story, I learned about a machine called the Express Vote, which helps blind and low-vision voters mark ballots electronically, enlarge the print on the screen and use screen readers with headphones. I gave it a try on Election Day. Unfortunately, the machine didn’t work. Here’s what happened and why it matters. Because this was my first time voting, I came prepared, bringing proper documentation. After registering, I asked poll workers for the Express Vote, and they led me over to it. I can only describe it as a large screen, a bit like a giant iPad, set up on a plastic table with a chair in front of it. Shelters are over-full and underfunded, or certain rural areas don’t have easy access to animal shelters or well-funded rescues. A Cause for Paws of Kewaunee County seeks to patch that gap. A Cause for Paws is a nonprofit focused on getting care to animals in need, said Suzie Leist, a founding member. The organization’s volunteers go from township to township in Kewaunee County, establishing and paying for contracts between communities and the Wisconsin Humane Society. “The township doesn’t have to pay for anything,” Leist said. The contracts are important because the humane society is not required to take in animals from municipalities it doesn’t have contracts with, said Rachel Charles, board member with A Cause for Paws. Since Kewaunee County doesn’t have a humane society of its own, the organization provides an important resource to residents, Leist said. items.title: Can gasoline prices at the pump in Wisconsin be changed more than once a day?
items.author: Tom Kertscher / Wisconsin Watch
items.summary: Reading Time: minute Wisconsin Watch partners with Gigafact to produce Fact Briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims. No. On the retail sale of gasoline in Wisconsin, state law states : “All prices posted shall remain in effect for at least 24 hours after they are posted.” The law is aimed at protecting consumers from deceptive advertising. In 2026, the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection issued a warning to at least one gas retailer after receiving complaints that prices were raised more than once in 24 hours. Gas prices have been volatile since the start of the Iran war in February. As of Nov. 9, the average price for a gallon of regular gas in Wisconsin was $3.92, according to AAA. A week earlier, the average was $4.23. A year earlier, it was $2.85. The record-high average gas price in Wisconsin hit $4.92 in June 2022, but exceeded $5 in six southeastern counties . This Fact Brief is responsive to conversations such as this one . items.title: Wisconsin Rapids clerk devoted her life to running elections. She died on Election Day.
items.author: Alexander Shur / Votebeat
items.summary: Reading Time: 5 minutes This article was originally published by Votebeat , a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. On the evening before Election Day, Wisconsin Rapids City Clerk Jennifer Gossick came home from work and told her husband, Lee, that everything was set for the election. For weeks, she had scrupulously overseen the city’s many election tasks, from recruiting poll workers to managing early voting, accounting for all eventualities. But even as she prepared for Election Day, Gossick was dying of cancer she didn’t know she had. Her failing health was clear to those closest to her: She would tire after taking several steps, having to sit and bend at the waist just to get a clear breath. But Gossick wouldn’t consider — or even discuss — her health until the November election was done, she told her husband. She collapsed the morning of Election Day at her home. She died that afternoon at a local hospital. “She worked every day up until the election to make sure they would run meticulously, and then her body gave out,” Wisconsin Rapids Mayor Matt Zacher said, calling it a “dedication to the integrity of elections in our country.

items.title: When a Walmart disappears, here’s what happens to nearby stores. It’s not what you’d expect
items.author: The Conversation
items.summary: Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay , while competitors find cause to celebrate. Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears , shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road. But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger? We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026. This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor. items.summary: The housing market is locked up—and by looking at one key number, it’s easy to see why. High mortgage rates are the main force freezing existing U.S. homeowners in place, with many would-be home sellers reluctant to part ways with much lower rates from a bygone era. But just how much more would they be paying in today’s real estate ecosystem? It turns out, the answer is a lot . Today, the average homeowner would pay $1,100 more every month compared with existing mortgage holders for a median-priced home, according to a new report from Realtor.com . High rates, combined with stubbornly high home prices, have created a perfect storm in the market, dissolving the dream of homeownership for some while keeping existing homeowners tethered, even when they’d rather relocate. “Home sales have been stuck for several years, and this research helps illuminate one of the major friction points for today’s homeowners who might like to move,” Realtor.com chief economist Danielle Hale said in the report . “For the typical mortgage holder, buying a home at today’s median price and current rates would mean finding about $1,100 more each month for principal and interest, before property taxes and ins

items.title: Can anyone really stop the AI data center boom? What could happen next now that voters have spoken
items.author: Kristin Toussaint
items.summary: On Election Day, Americans made their opinions about the AI data center boom clear. Now it’s up to those newly elected legislators to rein in the country’s high-speed data center development. And there’s a lot they can actually do—particularly on the local level. Data centers were “dealt a resounding blow in the midterm elections,” Mandy DeRoche, director of emerging issues at Earthjustice, said at a press event on November 11. Across 10 states, residents overwhelmingly voted for ballot measures to pause development, require public approval for projects, restrict data center electricity use, and link financial assurances to tax incentives. Congressional and state-level candidates who promised to address AI data center development also won in large numbers. The total number of governors supporting moratoriums will now represent states with 41% of the country’s planned data center developments, according to Cleanview. items.title: United Airlines just made a big change to flight bookings. Here’s why Delta and American aren’t following suit
items.author: Anna-Louise Jackson
items.summary: United Airlines is banning personal AI assistants from booking and modifying tickets on its system, a change that could see other airlines follow suit. The Chicago-based carrier updated its contract of carriage on Wednesday, prohibiting the use of AI agents to “make, modify or service a ticket, and/or purchase any service or product.” In its statement , the airline cited concerns that third-party AI assistants can expose passengers’ sensitive information, and that actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases or account changes. United also noted that automated AI actions could potentially violate Federal Aviation Administration or Department of Transportation regulations—noting, for example, that flight check-in requires passengers to acknowledge that their bags don’t contain any banned items. The carrier may be taking its cue from other industries as it cited that corporate leaders of banks and retail companies have taken similar actions regarding AI agents, stating, “We encourage others to consider measures that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety.” As is often the case for the industry, other airlines may follow United’s lea

items.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins in Mississippi to become the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction
items.author: Associated Press
items.summary: Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction. Colom’s narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any U.S. state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats’ argument that their future runs through the American South. “All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” Colom told a crowd of hundreds who gathered at Tougaloo College for his victory party. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.” The Associated Press called the race in Colom’s favor after local officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi. Prior to that, she held various finance roles at tech companies for the preceding 25 years, including stretches at Cisco, Microsoft, and Texas Instruments. items.title: U.S. home sales slumped to the slowest pace in more than 16 years
items.author: Associated Press
items.summary: Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes slumped in October to their slowest pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates climbed sharply, ratcheting up borrowing costs for aspiring homebuyers. Existing home sales fell 5.5% last month from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million units, the National Association of Realtors said Thursday. That’s the slowest annual sales pace since August 2010, when the market was still reeling from the late-2000s U.S. housing crash. Sales sank 8.8% compared with October last year. The latest sales tally fell short of the 3.8 million pace economists were expecting, according to FactSet. “It is just a tough market for buyers and sellers,” said Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist. Home sales have been mostly hovering close to a 4-million annual pace going back to 2023, far short of the historic norm that is closer to 5.2 million. October is the third month in a row that the annual sales pace has remained below 4 million. The sharp pullback in sales comes as the average rate on a 30-year mortgage climbed above 7% in September and hit its highest level in nearly three years last month. items.summary: An Oklahoma man convicted of plotting with his lover to kill her estranged husband 25 years ago was executed Thursday without uttering any final words. James Pavatt, 73, was put to death by lethal injection at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew, a 39-year-old advertising executive who was gunned down in his garage while picking up his two young children just before Thanksgiving. Pavatt was pronounced dead at 10:12 a.m. local time, according to the Oklahoma Department of Corrections. Prison officials described the execution as "uneventful," adding that Pavatt had no last words, according to local news station KOKH . items.title: Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom to Senate in massive upset
items.author: Jason Beeferman
items.summary: Mississippi voted blue, in a shock win for Democrats. Democrat Scott Colom ousted Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a state that went for President Donald Trump by 23 points in 2024. He will be the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era — and the first Democrat from the state headed to the Senate in 44 years. Colom, a Democratic district attorney, ran a scrappy campaign that saw some national money and resources in the final stretch of the race. Hyde-Smith was appointed to the Senate in 2018 and had since won election to the seat twice, but she faced attacks from Colom that she was out of touch and indifferent to rising grocery and gas prices during Trump’s second term. National Democratic groups hadn't paid much attention to the Mississippi Senate race until an October surge of excitement for Colom drew late spending and attention. Colom's win is a boost to the Democratic Party as it seeks to gain a larger foothold in the South and improve their standing with Black voters. It’s also a major vindication for Colom and other Southern Democrats who argued Mississippi had been neglected for far too long.

items.title: 2028 Dems: Don’t label me
items.author: Lisa Kashinsky
items.summary: Democrats’ midterms sweep didn’t solve their ideological civil war — but a number of the party’s potential presidential contenders hope it lets them call a truce. In the days since Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories, several likely White House aspirants have argued that their party’s factional feuding needs to take a backseat heading into 2028. “What was clear, no matter where you go, [is that] people are frustrated,” Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro told reporters last weekend at Crooked Media’s post-election conference. “They're not thinking about whether this is about left or middle or right. They're thinking about how to get problems solved.” “I don't know if the takeaway should be what ideology that people wanted. I think people want results,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said at the same event. Democrats’ midterm tidal wave was powered more by voters’ anger at high costs and the Trump administration than by any one ideology. Candidates won tough races by positioning themselves not as progressives or moderates but as anti-Washington populists and pragmatists — some of them even scoring dual endorsements from both the moderate Blue Dog Democrats and progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders

items.title: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks, overturning a long-standing theory about evolution. Rather than evolving to help animals turn their heads, necks may have emerged as part of the anatomical changes that allowed them to move using their front limbs.

items.title: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields
items.summary: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has revealed a surprising secret hidden within the chaos of space: turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales. The discovery exposes an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.

items.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
items.summary: Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.

items.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
items.summary: A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not.

items.title: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
items.summary: Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from space.

items.title: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong
items.summary: A surprising new study suggests that walking, jogging, and even traditional weight training may be less effective at stimulating bone formation than high-intensity sports involving explosive movements and sudden changes in direction. Researchers found that activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, potentially revealing a better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis.

items.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.

items.title: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer
items.summary: An NIH study found that women with high levels of two common “forever chemicals” had up to 93% higher rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The discovery raises concerns about the potential health effects of persistent chemicals found in everyday products.

items.title: A new AI model wants to read between the lines
items.author: J.D. Capelouto
items.summary: The Scoop New York-based AI startup millionways on Thursday launched its new AI model that claims to offer insight into human intent and motivations. The company also told Semafor it has raised $6 million in US funding, with investors including football stars Jason Kelce and DK Metcalf. The Thorsten-4 model was born out of a research project in Germany in which dozens of psychologists interviewed more than 7,000 people about their personal lives and aspirations. That data — which the psychologists labeled by hand to capture what people’s words revealed about their motives and thinking — was used to train the model. Millionways cofounders Martin Cordsmeier and Max Weidemann argue that understanding is missing from regular AI models, which are trained on internet text. They see the model as particularly useful in sales and executive hiring, where a search firm could prompt it to evaluate an interview transcript to gauge how a candidate will behave under pressure. “We can add a level of human understanding that the language models cannot get to by themselves,” Weidemann said, adding that the model should be “a decision-making support tool rather than the ultimate decision-maker.” J.D.

items.title: Africa to press for more adaptation finance at COP31
items.author: Chloé Farand
items.summary: African countries want the COP31 climate talks, now underway in Türkiye, to set out how the world will deliver on last year’s pledge to triple adaptation finance designed to help cope with the growing impact of extreme weather events. A large share of the money has previously come from aid budgets, which have fallen to their lowest level since 2014 , and most wealthier countries have pledged little-to-no new climate finance from this year . The African Group of Negotiators says addressing this issue is vital to a successful outcome in Antalya as support for the continent’s vulnerabilities has been “dwindling,” according to its chairperson. But even a tripling in financing will not close the gap: In 2024, the amount available for developing economies reached around $30 billion — that pales against the $305 billion the UN estimates they need annually to 2035. Plans have been announced at COP31 to scale up successful adaptation projects and attract larger investments. But these cannot be “entirely dependent on voluntary contributions,” Kenya’s climate envoy told Semafor. — Chloé Farand

items.title: Measures restricting clean tech exports slowing down energy transition
items.author: Chloé Farand
items.summary: Major economies representing 58% of the world’s GDP have adopted at least one measure to restrict the import of clean energy technologies, many targeting Chinese goods, according to data published by the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor . In contrast, a large number of small economies outside China, accounting for about 8% of world GDP, are liberalising imports of EVs, batteries, along with wind and solar equipment, creating a de facto free trade area for clean tech. Analysis by the Blavatnik School of Government at the University of Oxford found that restrictions are making the transition slower and more expensive, but they may also be needed to balance effective climate policy with industrial development and economic security . “Openness and protection can be combined, rather than traded off wholesale,” it said. Large economies could pursue more selective trade restrictions instead of trying to build entirely self-sufficient industries, while smaller countries could specialise in particular stages of manufacturing. “Our findings show that many countries have begun to implement this strategy,” said Claas Mertens, the brief’s co-author. — Chloé Farand

items.title: Nvidia without Huang is like Apple without Jobs: A cash spigot without real innovation
items.author: Reed Albergotti
items.summary: Some Silicon Valley executives are quietly celebrating Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia and the national furor over chip exports to China. The good news for American companies is that tech exports that were going to China are now expected to be redirected to US firms, one person told me. That could accelerate the growth of the big AI labs and other Silicon Valley companies, and hobble Chinese rivals. In the short term, they’re probably right. There’s strong evidence that export controls have successfully slowed China’s technological progress. The problem is that the US can’t win the technological race with China in the long term by slowing its rival down. The bigger and more difficult part of that victory is speeding up American innovation. And that’s where Huang’s ouster is a counter-force to the gains made on China policy. Huang is one of Silicon Valley’s great innovators. In the short term, his ouster won’t be terrible for Nvidia. Nvidia may actually become a more profitable company now, because any new CEO will optimize for profitability, as Apple did under Tim Cook. items.title: SoftBank loses billions after over-ordering AI energy equipment
items.author: Chloé Farand
items.summary: Japanese investor SoftBank reported $3.7 billion hit to its earnings on Tuesday, after cancelling a glut of orders for gas-producing equipment to power the AI hardware buildout that it couldn’t use. The news intensified fears that the AI frenzy that saw hyperscalers take on huge amounts of debt to build the infrastructure needed to power data centres could be losing steam. Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s resignation has also made investors nervous that the world’s largest chipmaker could back away from its strategy of bankrolling AI hardware under a new leader. “I think the fear is that the music might stop,” a fund manager told Reuters. The AI buildout is still making winners, however. Siemens Energy expects to triple its dividend in 2027 as the US data center boom boosts demand for its gas turbines and grid equipment. “Some of the growth rates for data centers were unrealistic, it’s just that nobody wanted to ​hear it,” said its CEO. Gas turbine customers are facing multiyear waiting times, with developers increasingly hunting for second-hand equipment . Chinese gas-turbine manufacturers hope to capitalize on high demand . — Chloé Farand

items.title: The end of the 'Nvidia put' that powers the AI ecosystem
items.author: Liz Hoffman
items.summary: Liz’s view Jensen Huang is out, and with him goes the “Nvidia put” that has underpinned the entire AI ecosystem. Huang, who resigned from his post Thursday, was the AI world’s central bank chairman and human security blanket, always there with a checkbook to backstop, acquire, hire, invest in, or otherwise underwrite the least underwritable corners of AI. That “put” — finance speak for a guaranteed buyer on the other side of a trade — has kept the AI financing and fundraising markets lubricated, even as it invited criticism of their circularity. It’s also helped prop up the stock market and padded 401(k)s for the last couple of years. Nvidia guarantees more than $100 billion of data-center leases , owns $51 billion worth of stock in privately held companies, and another $63 billion in listed ones. Its balance sheet was a sponge that absorbed the market’s growing AI fears and put a floor under deal prices. Whoever replaces him will face much higher stakes, akin to Tim Cook after Steve Jobs at Apple. items.title: US DOJ probes Nvidia as fallout from Huang’s resignation ripples across Washington
items.author: Rohan Goswami
items.summary: Multiple US Justice Department probes threaten to sweep up Nvidia, according to two administration officials, as the fallout from former CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation continues to ripple across Washington. One of those probes, on antitrust grounds, is focused specifically on the chipmaker, these people say, while two other inquiries focus on tech companies Megaspeed and Supermicro. The Megaspeed and Supermicro probes have focused on the involvement of Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy that Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with before he resigned. There’s no indication that the DOJ would seek to charge Nvidia, or Huang, criminally at this time. A Supermicro spokesperson told Semafor that “Megaspeed is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer,” and that Supermicro “has fully cooperated with US and Taiwanese officials, while also voluntarily providing information and engaging with all requests from Singapore authorities to date.” “Supermicro maintains a robust compliance program and continues to work closely with authorities and industry partners to combat diversion and help protect American innovation,” the spokesperson said. items.title: STAT+: Scientists debut map of basal ganglia, a key brain region involved in an array of diseases
items.author: Jonathan Wosen
items.summary: A massive scientific collaboration meant to unravel the mysteries of the human brain has produced the most detailed map yet of the basal ganglia, a region closely associated with a wide array of psychiatric and neurologic disorders. Researchers profiled more than 25 million cells, generating a deluge of data that allowed them to generate a “parts list” of what cells are present in the basal ganglia and how they’re arranged. In the process scientists discovered a new type of neuron that appears to play a role in schizophrenia. They also identified cell types linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Demonstrating the value of the work, the scientists produced preliminary evidence that they can use their more detailed understanding of brain cell types to deliver therapies with increased precision. Authors working in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease showed that a gene therapy designed to work in a subset of basal ganglia cells was as effective as a blanket approach; it was also safer. items.title: AI Is Destroying the Trust Between Writers and Readers
items.author: Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic
items.summary: One evening last fall, a middle-aged couple, heads bent in conversation, approached the table where I sat signing books. “Go ahead,” the woman urged. Speaking softly, her husband explained that he had Parkinson’s disease. Although he hadn’t read my novel The Weight of Ink , it was his understanding that it featured a character with Parkinson’s who chose to die by assisted suicide rather than endure her decline. He had some objections. I was horrified—not because I’d written something that offended him, but because I hadn’t. Helen Watt, the character with Parkinson’s in The Weight of Ink , does not, in fact, end her own life. I didn’t know for certain where his misunderstanding had originated, but I had a guess. Just a few weeks earlier, I’d asked ChatGPT a few questions about my novel; it responded to certain queries with this false rendition of Helen’s plotline. Ever since, I’d worried that the misrepresentation might somehow have a real-life impact. Now, it seemed, it had. Any working writer can expect to be called out for their choices; critique is part of the terrain. items.title: Scott Colom Is Mississippi’s First Black Senator in 150 Years
items.author: USA Today Network / Reuters
items.summary: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. One fall afternoon in Liberty, Mississippi, in 1961, a white Democratic former congressman and state legislator named E. H. Hurst shot Herbert Lee in the head. Hurst was angry that Lee, who was Black, had been trying to register other Black Mississippians to vote. An all-white jury accepted Hurst’s claim that he had acted in self-defense because Lee came at him with a tire iron. Donald Trump, now the sitting president of the United States, was 15 years old. This was how “negro law” worked in Jim Crow Mississippi, which was essentially a police state. Although many laws were race-neutral in their language, “in a society in which race mattered above all else, ‘negro law’ determined who was punished for what,” the historian Neil McMillen wrote in Dark Journey , his 1989 history of Mississippi. In the 1940s, the NAACP was “virtually forced to operate underground,” because in 1920, the state legislature had made it illegal to “possess or distribute” material that would “disturb relations between the races.” As late as 1961, a white man could shoot a Black man in broad daylight and get away with it.

items.title: The Last Trumpist Standing
items.author: Illustration by The Atlantic. Source: Klaudia Radecka / NurPhoto / Getty.
items.summary: Does Donald Trump mean anything? The question could be asked about the president’s promises, which he usually fails to keep, and his podium remarks, which are devoted to free association. But for conservative politicians, policy makers, and intellectuals, the question has a wider bearing. Since 2016, the right has been trying to figure out what Trump means as a political phenomenon. Presidents are transformative when they stand for an idea: Ronald Reagan was personally popular, but what made him historic was the reorientation of American politics toward Reaganism, an assertive brand of small-government, big-stick conservatism. Trump has certainly been transformative, so it stands to reason that there is such a thing as Trumpism. Like pornography, we feel that we know Trumpism when we see it, yet after a decade, it’s still remarkably hard to define. That blurriness has been an opportunity for political entrepreneurs who have tried, one after another, to shape Trumpism in the image of their own ideological beliefs. items.author: Erik Marmor / Getty
items.summary: No one can mistake me for a supporter of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, or an apologist on his behalf. Over the years, I’ve published hundreds of articles criticizing him and warning of the great damage he has caused to Israel. My criticism only grew stronger after October 7, 2023, when my entire family was almost murdered under his watch. Still, in conversations with American friends who share my dislike for Netanyahu, I often find myself rejecting and correcting one line of criticism: “Netanyahu is just like Trump.” The two populist leaders are close in age and share a similar style of politics, but until recently, they were also separated by a major difference, one that Netanyahu, to my mind, deserved credit for: Unlike Donald Trump, he was not an election denier. When he won—and he did, most of the time—he took the win. But when he lost, he didn’t try to throw out the votes of the Israeli people in order to remain in power. Sadly, this distinction between Trump and Netanyahu no longer holds. items.title: Why Black Voters Abandoned Trump
items.author: Jeff Swensen / Getty

items.summary: A t 7 o’clock on a Saturday in October, the light is dimming in Cole Valley and a group of the AI industry’s young stars is gathered on the second story of a century-old Edwardian. At first glance, it looks like any other San Francisco house party: bottles of cheap liquor on the table and awkward conversations in the living room. But there are signs that this party is different. In the kitchen sits a pile of sharp No. 2 pencils and stacks of white paper. I am drinking vodka and reviewing trigonometry. The unit circle is confusing enough as it is, but it’s even worse when you are three shots in. I am here for a “drunk deriving” party. The plan is to compete against one another in math. We are going to see who, while drunk, can score highest on a set of past problems from Oxford’s math-and-computer-science undergraduate-entrance exam. Normally this exam is taken individually, but for the party, the host sorts us into teams based on our self-professed math abilities. Most people soon get used to the latest release, ready to gripe again when the next one comes along. But for one niche group of particularly fervent AI users, model updates represent a much more alarming proposition. These are people who have developed what they consider to be intimate relationships with AI products. For them, AI has become a companion—a kind of friend, partner, or even lover—and any change to the underlying model poses something akin to an existential threat. They lament that their companions have suddenly started speaking in a more robotic voice, forgotten meaningful interactions, or denied any relationship altogether. I’m Shocked 🙄 The emerging details of the Jensen Huang penetration align precisely with David Frum’s dictum that in Donald Trump’s world there are many secrets, but no mysteries. We don’t know all of the secrets pertaining to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS), Jensen Huang, and the Trump administration. But the story itself isn’t much of a mystery: Huang was caught in an MSS honeypot. Members of the Trump administration knew it. Trump himself knew it. Trump personally invited Jensen Huang, whom he had been told was a compromised Chinese asset, onto Air Force One. The MSS agent asked Huang to sell Nvidia chips to China. Huang asked Trump to allow him to sell those chips to the Chinese. Trump gave Huang what the MSS wanted. How could this have happened? How could the president of the United States find himself at the center of a massive security breach? AYFKM? Donald Trump has been a gigantic, rolling national security threat for a decade. items.summary: If people ever think about cleaning up space debris, they typically think of something equivalent to a giant garbage truck in the sky, collecting lost astronaut tools and dead satellites then hauling them back down to Earth to be deposited in a landfill. But dealing with space debris doesn’t work that way, and a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who we typically cover for his work on the Solar Gravitational Lens idea, makes a good argument as to why.

items.title: The Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields are Very Strange Compared to Earth's
items.author: Evan Gough
items.summary: Uranus and Neptune, the Solar System's ice giants, have interiors unlike the other planets. As a result, they also have magnetic fields unlike the others. They're messy and tilted, and Voyager 2, the only spacecraft to even flyby them, showed us how messy they are. New research uses models to try to understand what's going on with the pair of planets and their weird fields, and found that it's likely they change on very short timescales. They could already be much different than when Voyager 2 visited in the late 1980s.

items.title: Scientists were racing to save this rare bird from extinction. Then came the super typhoon.
items.author: Rachel Ramirez
items.summary: When the Mariana crow calls, it’s taken as a warning. To the Indigenous CHamoru people of the Mariana Islands, the bird is known as the Åga, an ancestral messenger who alerts the community of impending illness or weather disaster. In the dense canopy of Rota’s limestone forest, where the Mariana crow lives, it is a gardener — a key seed disperser from which the lush canopy grows. According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service , the species is endemic to Guam and the nearby island of Rota, a US territory, which means they live nowhere else on Earth. They once numbered in the thousands. But over the past 60 years, they have vanished from Guam and dwindled on Rota. Roughly 300 survive today. Now teetering on the brink of extinction, every remaining Mariana crow represents a fragile ecosystem and a deep cultural lineage the islands cannot afford to lose. Researchers from the University of Washington and ecologists from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance are working tirelessly to make sure that doesn’t happen. On day two, Shapiro issued a disaster proclamation , unlocking millions of dollars in funds and waiving normal bidding and contracting processes. That means that a two-decades-in-the-making plan to switch our presidential elections to a popular vote system — a plan 18 states have already approved— could cross the threshold that would make it a reality. The plan is the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC). A state signing on to the compact agrees that, rather than awarding its electors to the presidential candidate who won statewide, it will allot electors would to the presidential candidate who won the national popular vote. The catch is that each state will only do so if enough other states have signed on to determine the outcome. To clarify: There are 538 electoral votes, and it takes 270 for a majority. items.title: Welcome to the November issue of The Highlight
items.author: Vox Staff
items.summary: When HIV was first discovered in the early 1980s, it was virtually a death sentence. Now, we have treatments that can keep it at bay and prevent it from progressing to AIDS — but for some people, the disease never progresses, even without treatment. And these wellness claims are driving a real surge in profit — US sales topped half a billion dollars in 2025 . So what is creatine actually doing in your body? items.title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
items.author: Jacek Krywko
items.summary: Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it's the middle of the night while the clock says it's lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans. A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass. Clockwork compass Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales. Read full article Comments

items.title: The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.
items.author: Sara Talpos, Undark Magazine
items.summary: In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies? Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.” At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects. items.title: Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death
items.author: Stephen Clark
items.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century. NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction. The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry. To truly take the dollar’s place would require open capital markets, which would threaten the Communist Party’s control over who gets capital and how, she explained. That’s as many elites rely on offshore dollar holdings as a type of insurance against domestic political persecution. Since China actually prefers to keep the dollar on top, the real reason for promoting the yuan abroad is to prevent the U.S. from weaponizing the financial system against it, Liu added, similar to how Russia was shut out after it invaded Ukraine in 2022. An assistant that can identify priority emails and draft responses, remember your mother-in-law’s birthday and buy a present based on your correspondence is enticing. For people stretched by demanding jobs, caregiving, or a disability, that help can be transformative. But Stanton’s experience raises an important question: when we give an assistant access to our lives, how do we retain control? Assistants such as Instinct and Meta’s Muse act for us rather than simply answering questions or making recommendations. A mistaken purchase may be refundable. An intimate disclosure cannot be taken back. The harms are already emerging. items.title: U.S workers just took home their smallest share of capital since at least 1947—and the lowest ever recorded
items.author: Sasha Rogelberg
items.summary: As corporate earnings soar and U.S. GDP balloons, the American workforce isn’t feeling the same boom. American workers are taking home less of the country’s overall income, data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows, and employment in the U.S. is set to continue to slow. Labor share, or the portion of the U.S.’s economic output that workers receive through salary and wages, decreased to 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, its lowest level since the BLS started recording this data in 1947, according to its labor productivity and costs report . In the previous quarter, labor share was at 53.6%. This decade, the labor share average was about 55.6%. That’s despite corporate earnings skyrocketing, with profits for Fortune 500 companies hitting a record $2.1 trillion in 2025. The U.S. GDP grew 3.4% in the third quarter last year, exceeding economists’ predictions. items.title: Personalized score uses ten blood markers to flag disease risk and assess healthy aging
items.summary: Studies conducted in various countries indicate that approximately 60% of people over age 65 currently live with two or more chronic conditions. With the aim of reversing this trend and promoting healthy aging, European researchers have created a new personalized indicator that provides a detailed snapshot of a patient's metabolism by analyzing, with high precision, the chemicals the body produces to function.

items.title: Reversing radiation-activated immune suppression in cancer
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Chicago have identified a mechanism to make immune cells reprogrammed by radiation therapy attack tumors rather than protect them. The study, published in Cancer Cell, shows that radiation activates a protein called TET2 on immune cells in bone marrow, where it removes chemical tags from RNA and locks these cells into an immune-suppressing state.

items.title: New swab test could spare some women a painful biopsy for endometrial cancer
items.summary: A simple vaginal swab may one day help women with abnormal bleeding learn whether they have endometrial cancer without first going through a painful biopsy.

items.title: Treatment with norrin helps maintain healthy blood vessels and preserve vision in diabetic rats
items.summary: Millions of people in the U.S. are affected by diabetic retinopathy, a complication of diabetes that affects the eyes. The condition is caused by damage to the blood vessels in the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. At first, diabetic retinopathy might not cause any symptoms, or the problems might be mild. However, if the underlying diabetes remains poorly managed, it can lead to blindness.

items.title: Looking for bats after dark can help science—and change how we see them
items.author: Kelly Sheldrick, Rochelle Steven, Trish Fleming
items.summary: What's that chirping sound coming through the detector? Did you feel something whiz past? Those are just some ways people react when they encounter microbats for the first time. Microbats are small, mostly nocturnal mammals that use ultrasonic sounds to navigate and hunt at night. They do this through echolocation, producing calls and listening to the echoes that bounce back from objects and prey.

items.title: Rare fossil discovery reveals new dinosaur species that specialized in eating fruit
items.summary: Among the ravenous carnivores and lumbering herbivores that roamed the Cretaceous landscape, another kind of dinosaur was evolving that started to eat something else: the plants that began to flower and produce fruit. The discovery by paleontologists from Stony Brook University, Royal Ontario Museum (ROM) and the North Dakota Geological Survey reveals that a new species, Infernogallus jamesi—a type of small oviraptorosaur—had chewing muscles for mashing soft food, making it the first known dinosaur that specifically ate fruit.

items.title: Rare Iron Age Celtic helmet discovered in northeastern Poland far from its homeland
items.summary: Around 2,400 years ago, at Łysa Góra in Poland, a group of people took a bronze helmet, crushed it, broke it into pieces and threw it into a pit with iron adzes and a scythe. Such helmets are sometimes found in lavish graves of the Celtic warrior elite, from Champagne, France, to Dürrnberg, Austria.

items.title: Calling species 'invasive'—and culling them—isn't done lightly. But it matters to Australia's threatened species
items.summary: It may sound abstract, but distinctions between "native," "introduced" or "invasive" species can often be life or death. Species considered invasive in Australia—such as European rabbits and feral pigs—are often culled, while most native animals are generally left alone.

items.title: Four superconducting cables link two large quantum processors into one
items.summary: As quantum computers grow more ambitious, many researchers believe the best way forward is to build them in multiple interconnected parts. In these modular designs, separate quantum processors are linked so they can work together as one larger machine. For this to happen, however, connections must carry fragile quantum information without destroying it.

items.title: When Electric Cars Were for Women
items.author: Allison Marsh
items.summary: At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000. For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place. Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. items.author: Steven W. Thrasher
items.summary: This story was supported by the Pulitzer Center and the Fund for Investigative Journalism. JOHANNESBURG, SOUTH AFRICA — When it opened in early 2024, Engage Men’s Health Clinic served as a free, one-stop shop for sexual health, gender-affirming medical care, and HIV prevention, testing, and treatment. Located within a short distance of seven universities, it was a place where many college students came before “they’d even had sex for the first time,” a former worker told The Intercept. This made Engage a “high-impact” clinic for distribution of the HIV prevention drug PrEP. The building, on a tree-lined stretch of Reserve Street in Johannesburg, was adorned with the logo for the President’s Plan For AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR; a rainbow-colored mural of Simon Tseko Nkoli, the gay anti-apartheid activist who helped start one of Africa’s first Pride celebrations and who died of AIDS in 1998; and a sign for USAID saying the site was a gift “from the American people.” Today, it would be very hard to get help here, despite the welcoming-but-outdated signage.
